The title is designated as *Huayan* because this treatise takes the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as its primary authority. Among the five teachings discussed below, it belongs to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This is because it clarifies the nature [of man] through this very scripture. "Original" (yuan) means to investigate its root.

Because one wishes to exhaustively investigate the fundamental origin of man, it is called "Investigating the Origin of Man" (Yuanren). A question is asked: "In Buddhism, it is commonly said that sentient beings pervade the five destinies."
Question: For what reason does this treatise designate only the "original person" (*yuanren*)? Answer: The author of the treatise considers humans to be of the same category as himself.

Thus, the preface states: "I have now obtained this human body, yet I do not know [myself]. Furthermore, among the six realms of existence, the other five destinies possess an uneven distribution of suffering and pleasure and are incapable of practicing the path.
Therefore, he specifically exhorts humans. —From the Preface to the *Yuanjue* by Prime Minister Pei Xiu.
It is said: That which sentient beings traverse in coming and going consists of the six paths of existence. Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of deep obscurity and sorrow;
birds and beasts harbor the grief of flight and panic; the asuras are in the midst of anger; and the devas are immersed in pleasure.
Only through the human path can one rectify the mind and thoughts to advance toward Bodhi. All Buddhas of the three periods of time have attained enlightenment within the human realm.
The Buddha acted for this very reason. Once the origin of human beings is understood, the categories of the four sages and the six classes of ordinary beings can likewise be known.
A *lun* (treatise) refers to critical evaluation; it establishes hypothetical questions and answers to investigate profound meanings, and is therefore called a *lun*.
The myriad spirits are all in motion; each has its basis.
"The myriad spirits" refers to those belonging to the categories of feathered, furred, scaly, and shelled creatures, as well as insects and the like. "In motion" (*chun*) means movement.

By citing "insects," all beings born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation are encompassed. "Each has its basis" means that the basis is precisely their causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*). This is explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding sentient beings.

It is said: "Mental karma serves as the cause; the egg, womb, moisture, and transformation serve as the conditions. Thus the five aggregates arise. The *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states:
"If there are all worlds and all species—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation—they all receive their life and nature through lustful desire.
One should know that in saṃsāra, craving is the root. Furthermore, a verse from the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "With a perverted mind..."

They proceed toward the realm of desire. Those born from moisture and by transformation are stained by fragrance and location. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The egg-born arise solely through thought; the womb-born are due to emotional attachment; the moisture-born result from contact;
and the transformation-born respond to separation. The *Vajraśekhara-śāstra* states: "That which is born from a shell is called 'egg-born'; it belongs to the category of moving beings.

That which emerges from within a container is called 'womb-born'; it belongs to the category of those with desire. That which arises depending on moisture is termed 'moisture-born'. Regarding moisture-born...

"Combined induction" (*sāṃyogika*) refers to the category of rebirth destinies (*gati*). It does not depend on parents; rather, it arises suddenly from the convergence of one's own mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*). To have something emerge suddenly where there was nothing is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).

Transformation responds through separation; it is a provisional category. Transformation likewise arises from one's own conceptions: one mentally projects a superior realm and feels affection for that object.

Even those born by transformation are thus excluded from [the category of] "responding" (i.e., being born). Therefore, we know that among the classes of sentient beings, regardless of whether they are large or small, all take passionate attachment as their very foundation.
This citation of sentient beings serves as an analogy for human beings.
The myriad things are in constant flux, yet each returns to its root.
"The myriad things" refers to the various categories of the hundred grains, grasses, and trees. "In constant flux" describes their state of profuse growth.
Only when each thing possesses its own root can its branches and leaves flourish. This passage uses insentient objects as an analogy for human beings.

There has never been a case where there are branches and twigs without a root. How much less could that which is the most spiritually gifted among the Three Powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) be without a source?
If there is no root, how can there be branches and twigs? Even insects, plants, and trees still possess causes and conditions; how much more so for the Three Powers?
Among these, only humans are most intelligent. How could they lack an origin? As for the "Three Powers" (Sancai), they are Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.
"Power" (cai) refers to capability: Heaven possesses the power of movement; Earth possesses the power of generation and completion; and humanity possesses the power of discernment and reflection.
Furthermore, "to know others is wisdom; to know oneself is clarity. Knowing others is secondary;
knowing oneself is primary. In the subsequent passage where the true source is revealed, realizing that one's nature is identical to that of the Buddha constitutes wisdom and clarity.
By means of the fundamental, the secondary is encompassed, leaving nothing out.
I have now received a human body, yet I do not know from whence it has come; how then could I know where I shall go in the next world?
"I" refers to the provisional self composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). "Having received" means that there is something received and thereby this body is obtained.

That from which one comes is what was received in previous lives; according to the internal teaching, this refers to past karma and afflictions, tracing back through successive stages to the fundamentally enlightened *tathatā*.
"Another world" (*paraloka*) refers to future lives. "Destiny" (*gati*) means the act of moving toward or approaching.
That is to say, once this body has been cast off, to which realm will one be reborn? To the heavens? Or to hell?
Whether ascending or falling—since one does not know where the body came from, how can one know where it will go after death?
How can one possibly know the human affairs of the world throughout antiquity and the present?
"The world" refers to the horizontal dimension of space; "antiquity and the present" refer to the vertical dimension of time.

Human affairs are exceedingly complex, such as the excellence or depravity of customs, the establishment or collapse of ritual and music, and the success or failure of punishments and governance. To know that which the body derives from—

Coming from this life and proceeding to the next world—this is the matter of knowing oneself beforehand. Human affairs throughout the past and present of the world—this is the matter of knowing others beforehand. Taking one’s own person as the root and the past and present of the world as the branches: to prioritize the root and follow with the branches is not to lose their proper order. If one does not investigate and understand one's own person, yet wishes to know Heaven, it is like seeking the branches while neglecting the root. This is why the sages first established the Way of the Self and subsequently clarified the Way of Heaven and Earth. It is for this reason that the *Laozi* says: "The Dao gives birth to One; One gives birth to Two; Two gives birth to Three; Three gives birth to the myriad things. The "One" refers to the self; the "Two" refers to Heaven and Earth. One must first know the self before one can know Heaven and Earth. If one does not know the self, how can one know Heaven? If one does not know Heaven, how can one know the myriad things? If one does not know the myriad things, how can one know the Dao? Therefore, the sages first cultivated themselves and only then governed the state. If one knows oneself, one will surely know Heaven and Earth. Regarding the affairs of men throughout past and present, how could one possibly master them all?
Therefore, for several decades, I studied without a fixed teacher, extensively examining both internal and external teachings to trace back to my own person.
By tracing this back without ceasing, I finally attained its root.
Regarding the "Teacher of Impermanence," the *Book of Documents* states: "Virtue has no constant teacher; take what is good as your teacher.

Goodness has no constant master; harmonize with it through single-mindedness. Qingliang [Zongmi] says: "Take those who benefit me as friends; let all people be your friends. This also carries that same meaning. It is broad.
This means "extensive investigation," which refers to thorough research. Internally, it concerns the essential tenets of the Buddhist teachings;

externally, it concerns the texts of the Confucians, Daoists, and the hundred other schools. His resolve was to exhaustively investigate the very foundation of his own being. He traced its origins without ceasing.

Thus, he attained its fundamental source. Therefore, the Preface to the Commentary on the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* by the Master of Treatises states: "In my childhood, I devoted myself to the teachings of Lu (Confucius); in my youth, I investigated the ancient texts of Zhu (the Buddha).

In my practice of Chan, I encountered the Southern School; in my study of doctrine, I met this scripture. It further states: "I traveled to a hundred cities in search of teachers, and while seated, I explored the multitude of scriptures."
This is the matter at hand.

However, those who today practice the Way of Confucianism know only that, in the near term, it was their ancestors and parents who transmitted the physical form in succession, thereby receiving this body;
and in the distant past, that the primordial unity of *hundun* was divided into the two forces of Yin and Yang, from which the triad of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity arose.
The Three Primal Powers give birth to the myriad things. The myriad things and human beings alike take *qi* as their fundamental substance.
Below this, the various schools are described individually; first, the non-Buddhist teachings are discussed. "Ru" refers to Confucianism, with Confucius as its founder.

The Way refers to the Daoist teaching, for which Laozi is the primary authority. The intent of these two schools [Buddhism and Daoism] is that both take *qi* (vital energy) as the primordial beginning, from which humans and the myriad things gradually emerge.
Thus, in terms of the near, it is said that the patriarch transmits to the father, the father transmits to the son, the son continues the father, and the father continues the patriarch;

one thus receives this physical body. In terms of the distant, it is said that prior to heaven and earth, there was only the single, unified *yuanqi* (original vital energy), which existed in a state of undifferentiated chaos.

They were not yet divided; hence they are called "chaotic" (*hundun*). To "cleave" means to divide and distinguish. After the chaos had been divided, the yang-qi was light and clear, and thus ascended;
the yin-qi was heavy and turbid, and thus descended. That which ascended became Heaven; that which descended became Earth.
The two qi harmonize and unite; human beings are born within them, forming the Three Powers (the Heaven, Earth, and Human).

From this, the myriad things gradually come into being. The *Daode jing* says: "The Dao gives birth to One; One gives birth to Two; Two gives birth to Three; Three gives birth to the myriad things. "One" refers to the pneuma of emptiness (*chongqi*).
This means that when the Dao moves and produces the wondrous pneuma of harmonious emptiness, it is still insufficient for the principle of generating beings, and thus it further gives birth to Yang.
Qi. Yang qi cannot arise alone; it also gives rise to yin qi. Because one accumulation of the primordial qi (chong qi) occurs, it is said that "One gives birth to Two.

Because two accumulations of yang qi occur, it is said that "Two give birth to Three. When yin and yang contain and nurture one another and the primordial qi is harmonized, only then do the myriad things flourish and mature.
Therefore, it is said that "Three give birth to the myriad things. Furthermore, the *Zhouyi* says: "The Yi possesses..."

The Supreme Ultimate (Tàijí) gives birth to the Two Polarities (Liǎngyí). The Two Polarities give birth to the Four Images (Sìxiàng). The Four Images give birth to the Eight Trigrams (Bāguā). The Eight Trigrams determine good fortune and misfortune.
Good fortune and misfortune give rise to great undertakings. Furthermore, the *Guīmìng Jué* states: "The *Yī* has five 'Supremacies' (Tài):
first is Tàiyì, when the appearance and phenomena have not yet differentiated; second is Tàichū, when the primal qi (yuánqì) begins to sprout; third is Tàishǐ, when form..."
This is the beginning. Fourth is the Great Primal (Taisu): form undergoes transformation and acquires substance. Fifth is the Great Ultimate (Taiji): form and substance are already complete.
From this point, heaven, earth, and the myriad things gradually arise. This discussion synthesizes the essential meanings of these two schools into a single text.
Those who study the Buddha-dharma say only this: as for the near cause, one receives this human body by undergoing retribution according to the karma created in previous lives;
as for the distant cause, that karma in turn arises from delusion, proceeding through successive stages until it reaches the *ālayavijñāna*, which serves as the fundamental basis of the body.
This describes the internal teachings (*adhyātma-śāsana*). Although it speaks of the Buddha-dharma in general, the intent specifically refers to the provisional and Hinayāna;

"nearby" refers to the teachings for humans and devas, while "farther back" refers to the final phrase, the Hinayāna teachings. The *ālaya-vijñāna* refers to the Dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) teaching.

Among these three, the preceding does not encompass the succeeding, whereas the succeeding necessarily encompasses the preceding. As for the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*), it means that delusion further arises from grasping.

Thus they arise. Now, both delusions (*moha*) and attachments (*grāha*) each have two types. Regarding the two types of delusion: first, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the two types of attachment: first, attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*); second, attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). This means that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and so forth arise from a multitude of conditions and fundamentally lack intrinsic nature;
yet sentient beings do not understand this and reckon them as real—this is called attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Due to...
Because one clings to phenomena, one is unable to penetrate the principles and facts of all mundane and supramundane dharmas; this is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Within these five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), even the phenomena themselves cannot be found, let alone a sovereign self. Sentient beings falsely conceptualize a real self within them;

this is called the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*). Due to this clinging to a self, the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) arises, and the defilements compete to flourish, resulting in karmic retribution.
It does not cease; by means of this, one revolves in saṃsāra, and the fruits of suffering are inexhaustible.

While those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) merely eliminate the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consisting of the grasping at a self, they have not yet severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of the grasping at phenomena. Bodhisattvas, however, sever both types of grasping and both types of hindrance.
Now, these two types of grasping and two types of hindrance all possess seeds within the ālayavijñāna; from these seeds, the manifest [states] arise, giving rise to delusion.
Regarding the creation of karma: if one investigates its origin to the very root, it lies within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Thus, the phrase "even unto" (*nai-zi*) indicates that one has already thoroughly exhausted the principle; yet, in reality, this is not yet the case.
As stated above regarding the teachings of both internal and external schools, all are the expedient and gradual discourses of the sages; they are not the ultimate, definitive meaning.
Fearing that people might become dogmatically attached to them, I have refuted them collectively. My intention lies in reproaching the person, not in disparaging the Dharma.
However, Confucius, Laozi, and Śākyamuni are all supreme sages. Adapting to the times and responding to beings, they established teachings through diverse paths.
Internal and external traditions support one another, together benefiting the multitudes.

One might fear that an objection could be raised as follows: "The fundamental vital energy (*prāṇa*), yin and yang, karma, delusion, and the transformations of consciousness described previously are all teachings spoken by the supreme sages Confucius, Laozi, and Śākyamuni; how can they be rejected? Therefore, we now respond: At the time of Confucius and Laozi...
The faculties of the people in this land have not yet matured; they are not yet capable of hearing the discourse on cause and effect, let alone the definitive teachings on Buddha-nature.
Therefore, Confucius and Laozi first gradually guided them through benevolence, righteousness, and morality, while pointing to primal qi and yin-yang as the fundamental principles.
For forty years before the Buddha appeared in the West, the faculties of the people had not yet matured and were not yet capable [of receiving such teachings].

Having heard the definitive meaning of the Buddha-nature, it is for this reason that the Great Awakened One provisionally followed the capacities of those of the three vehicles and five natures, speaking of the transformation of karmic consciousness and so forth; only after forty years did he finally preach the One Vehicle. Thus, the Lotus Sūtra says:

"For a long time I have kept silent regarding this essential point, not being in a hurry to speak of it. All of this manifests his responding to things according to the times. This refers to the phrase "different paths."
"Those" refers to divergent paths; this specifically indicates the previously mentioned primordial qi (*yuanqi*), karma, and delusions (*huo*).

Because the established teachings differ, they are called "divergent paths. Regarding the statement that the internal and external support one another: although the teachings established are different, they nevertheless rely upon and assist each other.
Buddhist teachings rely on Confucianism and Daoism as the initial means for guiding sentient beings; Confucianism and Daoism rely on Buddhism...
The teaching is the ultimate means for the perfection of all things; therefore, it is said that it brings benefit to the multitudes.
It encourages diligence in the myriad practices, clarifying the beginning and end of cause and effect; it investigates the myriad dharmas, revealing the origin and development of their arising.
Although these are all the intentions of the Sage, they contain both the provisional and the real.

Furthermore, one might fear that it could be objected: "Since the sages of the three teachings equally possess the heart that benefits sentient beings, all three teachings should be able to trace back to the origin of humanity.
Why, then, does this text exclusively take Buddhism as its primary authority? Therefore, he answers again: "As for the heart that benefits sentient beings..."

Although the three sages are identical in their ultimate aim, they differ in the application of their provisional and ultimate teachings. While Confucianism and Daoism are exclusively provisional, Buddhism encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate.

Since we now adopt the definitive meaning of the ultimate teaching, we exclusively take refuge in Buddhism. As for those who exert themselves in the myriad practices, the gates of practice are numerous;
it is not merely the exposition of giving, precepts, and so forth, but extends even to the Four Noble Truths, Dependent Origination, and the Ten [Wholesome Paths].
Excellent. The Five Precepts, the Four Dhyānas, the Eight Samādhis, the Five Constants of Confucianism and Laozi, and the Way and its Power (*Dao-de*) are all contained therein.
As for the beginning and end of cause and effect, only Buddhism clarifies this: cultivation of causes is the beginning, and the realization of effects is the end.

Furthermore, the origin and development of the myriad phenomena can also be discussed through the lens of the Three Teachings: Confucianism and Daoism take *qi* (vital energy) as their fundamental basis, while the Buddhist teaching takes...

Karma, afflictions, the eight consciousnesses, and True Suchness (tathatā) constitute the basis; according to the differences among the schools, their derivative manifestations can be understood accordingly.

While it is said that "all are the intent of the Sages," this is an expression of concession (longci); yet, regarding the presence of the provisional and the real, this is an expression of refutation (duoci).
The two teachings (the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles) are exclusively provisional (*upāya*).
The Buddha’s teaching encompasses both the provisional and the real (*bhūta*). "Provisional" means expedient or temporary; it is also called "expedient suitability.

Just as a scale-pan is called "provisional" because it can measure weight, it serves as a metaphor for the Sage’s skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) in discerning circumstances and bestowing the Way according to the capacity of the vessel. "Real" refers to the kernel of the fruit.
It takes its strength from being firm; it is what is called being solid and truly unshakeable.

If that is so, may we hear about the provisional means (*upāya*) of the two teachings and the provisional means of the Buddhist teaching? The answer is: there is a difference between the hidden and the manifest. As for the provisional means of the two teachings:
This is precisely the esoteric provisional [teaching]. The provisional teaching of Buddhism, however, is the exoteric provisional [teaching]. Why is this so? The Great Master Mingjiao said:

"As for the provisional, there is the exoteric provisional and the esoteric provisional. The exoteric provisional constitutes the shallow teaching and the small path; the esoteric provisional constitutes the heterodox way and other teachings.
Regarding the shallow teaching, there are the Dharma-characteristics (Hossō) and the Shattering of Characteristics (Hosshō) schools. As for the small path...
The cases of the two vehicles, humans, and devas are the Buddha’s teachings given according to what is appropriate; therefore, these are called "manifesting the provisional.

As for "concealed provisionality," it refers to the wondrous functioning that is without fixed form, arising secretly and responding mysteriously: sometimes acting as a teacher of heterodox paths to transform those of such a class;
or sometimes acting as a master of other doctrines, employing their own teachings to benefit the world. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Or..."
Whether one observes the precepts of the ox, the dog, or the deer; wears tattered robes;

or serves the sacrificial fire—by exerting oneself in myriad practices and restraining evil while encouraging good, all paths lead to the same governance. Thus, the three teachings may all be followed.
To seize [the mind], one first lets it loose; this demonstrates the function of provisional teachings.

Whether it be the Three Bonds and Five Constants of Confucianism, the preservation of the female and the maintenance of weakness in Laozi’s school, or the Three Studies and Six Perfections of Buddhism—none of these fail to cause people to exert themselves in the cultivation of myriad practices.
It merely consists in ceasing evil and promoting good. While the methods of instruction differ, they converge upon the same goal of governance.
Since the ultimate goal is the same, following either path is acceptable. Therefore, by relying on Confucianism, one becomes a gentleman perfected in virtue; by following the teachings of Laozi...

Thus, one becomes a true person of pure stillness. By receiving the teachings of Śākyamuni, one emerges from the three evil realms to proceed toward the human and celestial realms, until finally realizing the three vehicles and perfecting the two fruits.
When one investigates the myriad phenomena, exhausts their principles, and realizes their nature until reaching the fundamental source, only then does Buddhism provide definitive resolution.

The preceding [discussion] employed both concession and refutation to manifest the function of the True Teaching (Shijo). My previous statement that the three teachings are all worthy of adherence merely followed the Sage’s expedient means for benefiting beings;
it addressed the treatment of the human body once it was already formed, rather than intending to exhaustively investigate the ultimate source.
This is the fundamental source of becoming a person. If one wishes to exhaustively investigate this source, nothing but the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) can fully elucidate it.

Regarding the statement that "one examines the myriad phenomena (*dharmas*), exhausting principle and reaching the limit of nature": "examining" (*tui*) means seeking out their ultimate cause; "exhausting" (*qiong*) means reaching the very root;
and "reaching the limit" (*jin*) means exhausting the depths of their accumulation. "The myriad phenomena" refers to all worldly and transworldly phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

However, the expressions "exhausting principle" (*qiónglǐ*) and "exhausting nature" (*jìn xìng*) originate from the *Zhou Yi*. Its *Xici* (Appended Statements) says: "Exhaust principle and exhaust nature, thereby reaching destiny" (*qiónglǐ jìn xìng yǐ zhì yú mìng*).

Although this passage borrows that text, the intended meaning here is different. "Principle" (*lǐ*) refers to the way things are (*dàolǐ*) or ultimate truth (*zhēnlǐ*). "Nature" (*xìng*) refers to the nature of phenomena (*fǎxìng*) or the nature of the mind (*xīnxìng*);

it does not refer to what is bestowed by Heaven, and therefore the term "destiny" (*mìng*) is not used. This refers to the single dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which stands in horizontal opposition to all [phenomena].

"Phenomena" (*shi*) refers to the breadth of principle (*li*). "Vertical penetration of the single dharma" refers to the depth of nature (*xing*). Thus, when residing in the insentient, it is called *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena);

when residing in the sentient, it is called *cittatā* (the nature of mind), also termed *buddhatā* (Buddha-nature), also named *mūlajñāna* (original enlightenment), and also called the *tathāgatagarbha* (womb of the Tathāgata).
This is precisely the true nature (*bhūtadharmatā*) taught in the teachings that reveal the nature below. It means that all phenomena, such as form and mind, from...
They arise through conditions and lack any real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). They are entirely formed by True Suchness (*tathatā*) following conditions;
therefore, these myriad phenomena all take True Suchness as their source. Thus, the Preface to the Commentary on the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states:

"The myriad phenomena are false and illusory, arising through the convergence of conditions. The phenomena that arise are fundamentally non-existent; all is but consciousness. Consciousness is like an illusion or a dream; it is merely..."

With a single mind, one knows through the stillness of the mind; this is termed "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*). This refers to tracing all phenomena back to their original source. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"This ultimate meaning of all phenomena is also True Suchness (*tathatā*); because it is eternally as it is in its own nature, it is the true nature of all phenomena.
This is precisely that same meaning. To speak of reaching the original source does not mean departing from the Truth.

Apart from this nature, there is no separate source; however, because the teachings distinguish between shallow and deep levels of expression, there is the distinction between reaching and not reaching [this reality].
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "The True Suchness of the Mind is the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm.
That is to say, the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished... and so on, until it says: 'It is solely this One Mind,' and is therefore called 'True'."
Furthermore, it is said: "The Mahāyāna, in general, is of two kinds: first, the phenomena (dharma); second, the meaning (artha).
What is called 'phenomena' refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena."
Based on this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "How are the aggregates (skandhas) described?
What is the nature of the aggregates? The nature of the aggregates cannot be extinguished; therefore, they are said to be unarisen (*anutpāda*).

When these aggregates are analyzed, their nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent. Because they are empty, they cannot be extinguished; this is the meaning of non-arising. Since sentient beings...

It is thus. The Buddhas are likewise so. Since the Buddha and all Buddha-dharmas are by nature non-existent, one knows that the wondrous nature of *tathatā* (suchness), which is neither born nor extinguished, is truly the fundamental source of all dharmas.
How could this be reached except through the definitive meaning of the One Vehicle? "Definitive" (*niyata*) means a determined and settled meaning; it also implies a decisive and manifest revelation.
However, scholars of the present day each cling to a single school. Even those who take the Buddha as their teacher remain deluded regarding the true meaning;
consequently, they are unable to trace back to the ultimate source of heaven, earth, humanity, and things.
This first clarifies that other schools have not yet attained full understanding; it serves as the occasion for composing this treatise.

"Scholars" refers generally to those who study the three teachings, each adhering to a single school—meaning those who study Confucianism adhere solely to the Mandate of Heaven, while those who study Daoism adhere solely to spontaneity (*ziran*), and so forth, no longer investigating broadly or achieving comprehensive mastery. "Those who follow the Buddha" specifically refers to the insiders [Buddhists].

Those who practice the provisional teachings of our school either cling to karma and afflictions, or cling to the transformation of consciousness; they do not believe in the One Vehicle’s true teaching.
Even when discussing Buddha-nature, they invariably exclude the icchantika; even when speaking of True Suchness, they speak only of its unchanging aspect.

Because there is something they have not yet awakened to, it is said that they "remain deluded. They are like a group of blind men feeling an elephant: how could they know the elephant's entire body? They sit within a well...

When observing the heavens, can one truly perceive their boundlessness? Here, I first rely on what is known by those under instruction to clarify the provisional and the ultimate aspects of the Exoteric Teaching;
now, based on the attachments held by those under instruction, I provide the opening for the composition of this treatise.
I now once again rely upon the principles of both internal and external teachings to investigate the myriad dharmas.
By relying on these internal and external principles, one’s understanding becomes perfectly integrated, free from the defect of partiality or narrowness;
thus, the distance between such a person and those who have never read Buddhist scriptures yet presume to discuss Buddhism is vast indeed.
Initially, one proceeds from the shallow to the profound. For those who practice the provisional teachings, one dispels their stagnation to enable penetration and reaches the ultimate source.
Subsequently, relying on the definitive teachings, one reveals the meaning of successive origination, harmonizing the partial to make it perfect, and arrives at the final consummation.
"From the shallow to the deep" refers to the first two gates of the treatise, which refute deluded attachments that are biased and superficial;
herein, each preceding stage is shallow while each succeeding stage is deep. "Refuting stagnation to bring about penetration" means shattering clinging emotions to reveal perfect understanding.
"Reaching its ultimate source" refers to the third gate, which reveals the true origin. This is displayed by relying on the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Regarding "arising through successive transformation": this refers to the fourth section, which employs the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) to reveal the nature [of reality] and harmonize it with what was previously grasped, establishing them as a single truth.
This text consists of four chapters and is titled "The Origin of Man."
This concludes the title of the summary. The preceding introductory section is finished. As for the four chapters: first, refuting deluded attachments; second, refuting partiality and superficiality;
third, directly revealing the true source; and fourth, harmonizing and integrating the fundamental and the derivative.
First, the refutation of deluded attachments (referring to those who practice Confucianism and Daoism).
"Refutation" means to expel and cast out. "Deluded" refers to being confused and lacking awakening. "Attachment" refers to stubbornly adhering to a position without wavering.
The two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism state that all categories of beings, including humans and animals, are generated and nurtured by the Great Way of Non-being (*xūwú dàodào*).
This section below demonstrates the great concordance between these two schools. A Daoist scripture says: "There was a thing, a chaotic unity, born before heaven and earth.
It was silent and vast, standing alone and unchanging; it circulates everywhere without exhaustion, and may be called Heaven."
It is the "Mother below. I do not know her name; I have provisionally named her "the Way" (*Dao*). Furthermore, that scripture says: "The Way gives birth to them;

Virtue nurtures them; things give them form; and circumstances bring them to completion. All of this speaks of the function of the Great Way of Non-being (*xūwú*) in generating and nourishing all things.

This means that the Way (Dào) takes spontaneity (zìrán) as its principle. It gives rise to the primal qi (yuánqì); the primal qi gives rise to heaven and earth; heaven and earth give rise to the myriad things.
This explains the sequence of origination by inferring from the two schools [of thought]. The term "this means" (*yuè wèi*) refers to the essential purport of these two schools.

The phrase "the Way takes spontaneity as its principle" is derived from the *Dàodé jīng*. It says: "Man models himself on the Earth; the Earth models itself on Heaven; Heaven models itself on the Way; the Way models itself on..."
"Spontaneity" (*zìrán*) refers to the Great Way of Non-being mentioned above. "Spontaneity" is the nature of the wondrous source;
since this nature is not something produced through effort, it is called spontaneous. "The Way" (*dào*) is the function of the wondrous source.

"The Way" and "spontaneity" are designations for essence and function, which differ from the aforementioned [usage]. This follows the method of the text's phrasing; it does not mean that the Way imitates spontaneity.

Furthermore, that scripture states: "One gives birth to two; two give birth to three; three give birth to the myriad things. Now, when it is said that [the Dao] gives birth to the primal qi (*yuánqì*), this corresponds to the "Dao giving birth to one" of that text.
When the primal qi gives birth to heaven and earth, this corresponds to the "one giving birth to two" and "two giving birth to three.

When heaven and earth give birth to the myriad things, this corresponds to the "three giving birth to the myriad things. This refers to the "chaotic state" (*hùnzhùn*) mentioned in the preceding narrative.
This refers to the teachings of the Confucianists; this speaks of the Great Way (Dàodào). It also conveys the intent of the Master of Old (Lǎozǐ).
By citing these two in succession, it reveals the great concordance between the two traditions.

Therefore, whether one is wise or foolish, noble or lowly, poor or wealthy, and whether one experiences suffering or joy—all are received from Heaven and depend upon the timing of one's destiny (*kāla-vipāka*).

Regarding the fact that the various categories among humanity differ and are said to "receive [their lot] from Heaven" and "depend upon the timing of their destiny," the Confucian school generally says:
"Life and death are determined by destiny; wealth and honor are in Heaven. It is further stated: "That which acts without being acted upon is Heaven."
That which arrives without being sought is destiny (*ming*).
Therefore, after death, one returns to heaven and earth, restoring oneself to emptiness and non-being (*wu*).

The former [section] was a summary of how things arise from the root to their branches; this is a summary of tracing back to the origin and returning to the end. Heaven and earth are that to which the Confucian tradition ultimately reverts.
As for "returning to nothingness" (*xūwú*), it is what the Master of Old (Laozi) restored. The *Daodejing* says: "All things, in their profusion, return to their root.

Returning to the root is called stillness; stillness is called returning to one's destiny. This means that once all things have received the primal qi of Heaven and Earth to come into being, they flourish like grasses and trees depending on their roots.
When they die, they return to their original source, just as grasses and trees wither and fall.
The vital essence returns to its original root; this is restoring that which was received as one's innate nature and destiny.
To be born from Heaven and Earth and to return again to Heaven and Earth is as Shao Yong said: "Heaven gives me birth; Heaven takes me back in death.
To submit entirely to Heaven—what could be more appropriate? This is precisely what is meant by this.
However, the fundamental tenets of external teachings consist merely in establishing conduct based upon the body; they do not concern themselves with the ultimate origin of the body.

By "external teachings," one refers to Confucianism and Daoism—that is, those outside of the Buddha-dharma. The Confucian school emphasizes the five constant virtues and the hundred forms of conduct, while the Laozi school maintains the female principle and guards the state of weakness;
both are concerned solely with the cultivation and adornment of the person. They do not speak of why this body exists.

There is. Why does one become human? Why does one become an animal and so forth? Even if one were to explain the underlying causes, they would not go beyond the primordial vital energy (*yuanqi*) of the Great Way.
As for all things that are spoken of, none are considered to exist outside of this.
"Xiang" (image) refers to the form and appearance of things. Heaven and earth are both contained within these images.
What the teachings of the present world discuss as the greatest does not exceed heaven and earth; yet humans, animals, and the myriad things all exist within heaven and earth.
Therefore, their discourse never goes beyond the realm of heaven and earth. Zhuangzi said: "As for that which lies outside the six directions, the sage leaves it to exist [without investigating it]."
Since they do not discuss it, we know that it is not that Confucius and Laozi truly did not know what lies beyond heaven and earth;

rather, it is simply because the wisdom of worldly people is shallow and insufficient for such deliberation. As the *Analects* says: "The Master’s words concerning human nature and the Way of Heaven were things one could not hope to hear.
How much less, then, could he speak of that which transcends these phenomena?
Although it points to the Great Way as the fundamental basis, it does not fully clarify the causes and conditions of compliance and opposition, arising and ceasing, or defilement and purity.
I fear there may be those who ask: "The two traditions of Confucianism and Daoism also speak of the Great Way, the primal qi, and so forth as generating all things."
This, then, is the primordial qi of the Great Way; it is the very foundation of the body. How can you say that its origins have not been investigated?

Therefore, the present commentary states: "Primordial qi, the mandate of Heaven, parents," and so forth, are merely the instruments for producing the body, but they are not the body's foundation itself.

It is like a young child who sees his mother with a basket and a steamer and, taking a cake from them, eats it; he then knows that these are the basket and the steamer [but not the source of the cake].
It is formed by means of a steamer. Later, when one asks for bread, one points to the steamer basket;

yet how could one know that the steamer basket is merely the instrument for making the bread, and not the very origin of the bread? Now, the primal qi and heaven and earth are what is meant by the "steamer basket.
To grasp them as the fundamental basis of the self is merely the view of a child. That you do not fully clarify this and so forth is precisely [the case].

This reveals what the two schools are deluded about. Regarding "arising and ceasing in accordance with or against [the flow]": this refers to the twelve links of dependent origination as taught in our own school (Buddhism).
When one is deluded, volitional formations arise from ignorance, proceeding successively until birth, old age, and death;

this is the arising and movement in accordance with the cycle of birth and death, resulting in transmigration. When one attains awakening, one contemplates in reverse order from old age and death back to ignorance.
Thereupon, one gives rise to wisdom and severs ignorance. Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease, and so on, until birth, old age, and death cease;

thus one attains the fruit of the noble ones. This clarifies the process of returning to cessation by reversing the cycle of birth and death. These twelve links are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles;

their meanings and categories are so vast and extensive that they cannot be fully exhausted here in brief. Regarding the causes and conditions of defilement and purity, there are two [aspects]. First:
Regarding the Hīnayāna, its exposition is twofold. First, as in the aforementioned twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*):

from ignorance (*avidyā*) as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), up to birth (*jāti*) as the condition for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), these are the causes and conditions of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). From the cessation of ignorance leading to the cessation of volitional formations, up to the cessation of aging and death, these are the causes and conditions of purification (*vyavadāna*).
Second, regarding the Four Noble Truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*) of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path: namely, suffering and its origin.

These are the causes and effects of the mundane world. Cessation and the Path are the causes and effects of the supramundane. Because one accumulates the cause of the Truth of Origination, one experiences the fruit of the Truth of Suffering;
this is termed a defiled causal condition. Because of weariness with suffering, one gives rise to the wisdom of the Truth of the Path and severs that cause of origination.

The fruit of suffering does not arise; realizing the principle of the Truth of Cessation is called the "pure condition. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says: "From delusion comes craving, and from this my illness arises;
when the illnesses of sentient beings are cured, my illness is also cured. Second, regarding the Mahāyāna, there are likewise two [aspects].

First, according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school (Faxiangzong): it is held that the ālayavijñāna naturally encompasses the seeds of the names and conventions of the three vehicles (triyāna) and the three natures (trisvabhāva).

However, all sentient beings differ in whether these [seeds] exist or not. If one possesses the seeds of the three vehicles, upon encountering conditions for perfuming (vāsanā), one cultivates practice to sever hindrances and shall attain the noble fruits of the three vehicles; this is termed the "pure cause-condition" (viśuddha-hetu-pratyaya). (This refers, for now, to the three vehicles...)

[The general statement should be explained specifically: If there are no seeds of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), but only the seeds of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) with outflows (*sāsrava*), one then performs the three kinds of karma—meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—and wanders through the three realms;
this is called the defiled cause and condition. Second, according to the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-naya*).

The union of the true and the false constitutes the *ālaya-vijñāna*. When one is deluded, the defiled dharmas (which are the aforementioned falsehood) possess power while the pure dharmas (which are the aforementioned truth) lack power;
thus, one turns downward toward conditions and sinks through the three realms of existence—this is termed the "defiled causes and conditions.

When one awakens, the pure dharmas possess power while the defiled dharmas lack power; thus, one turns upward away from conditions and attains the four stages of the noble ones (the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas).

The name "Pure Causes and Conditions" (Jing yinyuan) has been heard of extensively, as cited below. How could those outside the Buddhist teachings know such Dharma meanings, much less be able to explain them fully?
Therefore, practitioners should not treat such provisional designations as definitive truths and cling to them as final realizations.

What Confucius and Laozi taught was merely provisional; if one does not cling to it, it serves as a condition for entering the Way, but if one clings to it dogmatically, it becomes a hindrance that obstructs the Way.
Guifeng said: "Confucianism provides the foundation for the precepts, and Daoism assists in *dhyāna*; these are its conditions.
Among the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*), being worldly-wise, eloquent, and clever conversely constitutes a difficulty; this is its obstruction.
Now, I shall briefly set forth and interrogate [these positions].
Regarding the refutation of the two schools, the following text consists of four parts: first, the refutation of the arising of the Way (*dao*), which is held by the Daoist school;

second, the refutation of spontaneity (*ziran*), which is held by the Daoist school and also by the Confucian school; third, the refutation of primordial pneuma (*yuanqi*), which both the Confucian and Daoist schools hold.
The fourth point challenges the mandate of Heaven as held by the Confucians.

Regarding their claim that all things arise from the Great Dao: the Great Dao is the very root of life and death, of the worthy and the foolish, and the foundation of good fortune and misfortune, of calamity and blessing.
This is a refutation established by Dao-sheng against the tenets of external schools.
If the fundamental [nature] were to exist eternally, then calamity, disorder, wickedness, and folly could not be eliminated, and blessings, fortune, worthiness,
and goodness could not be increased.

Since the Dao is eternal, all things should likewise be eternal. Just as descendants resemble their ancestors, so too should calamity and disorder be eternal, such that they could not be eradicated by human effort;
and blessings and prosperity should likewise be eternal, such that they could not be increased through the accumulation of goodness.
Thus Li Sishen said: "Laozi [taught] that life and death are destiny; all are the workings of the Dao."
The nature of the sage and the unworthy is that which is bestowed by Heaven; what Heaven bestows cannot be escaped, and the Way cannot be defied.
One who knows that the Way of Heaven cannot be escaped or defied is able to dwell in peace within long life.
What need is there for the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi?
The Sage perceives that goodness brings benefit and can lead to fortune; therefore, he teaches people to do good. He perceives that evil brings harm.
This can lead to calamity; therefore, the teachings urge one to distance oneself from evil.

If one claims that all things are created by the Dao, then tigers and wolves are beasts that harm humans—the Dao nurtures them and causes them to do so. Jie and Zhou were rulers who oppressed the people—the
Ran was virtuous yet did not enjoy a full lifespan; the Dao brought about his premature death. Yi Yin and Shu Qi were virtuous yet met with calamity and died;
the Dao brought about their misfortune. The *Daodejing* states: "Of all things, none do not revere the Dao and honor Virtue.
If that which the Dao does is truly as described here, how can it be called "revered"?

Furthermore, as for the claim that all phenomena arise through spontaneous transformation (*svabhāva*) and are not produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), this is another instance of establishing an objection based on the fixed tenets of non-Buddhist schools regarding spontaneity. The internal teaching (Buddhism) states that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions:
that which can directly initiate [an effect] is called the cause, while that which can indirectly assist in its arising is called the condition. It is like grass...
Trees and the like arise from seeds; these are called the direct cause (*upādāna-hetu*). Water, soil, humans, and time are called the indirect conditions (*pratyaya*).
Humans, animals, and so forth, arise from karma and delusion; these are called the direct cause. Parents and the two vital energies (*śukra-śoṇita*) are called the indirect conditions.
Since those followers of Confucianism and Daoism maintain that things are spontaneous (*svabhāva*), they do not investigate causes and conditions. Thus, Zhuangzi said: "I do not know why."

However, this is called "spontaneity" (*ziran*). It is further said: "The crane is white without bathing; the crow is black without being soot-stained. These are said to be all matters of spontaneity.
Regarding the Confucian tradition, Sima Junshi’s *Eulogy on Non-Action* (*Wuwei zan*) states:

"Advancing and retreating follow the Way; gain and loss follow destiny. To maintain the Way lies within oneself; when success is achieved, it is due to Heaven. What more does Heaven do? Everything is nothing but spontaneity."

Then, in all places where there are no causes and conditions, everything should arise through transformation; that is to say, stones should produce grass, grass should produce humans, and humans should produce animals and so forth.
Since nothing would depend upon causes and conditions, stones—which are not the causes and conditions for grass—should be able to produce grass, and grass should produce humans.
Human beings, domestic animals, and so forth—because these are all not conditions [for one another].

As for the phrase "and so forth," it includes all things that are not conditions, such as fire producing grass and trees, or wood producing fish and birds; that is to say, all instances where production would be inappropriate.
All are capable of being produced. This refers specifically to the case where a person arises without depending on the conditions of parents, suddenly manifesting as a human being or the like.
This is the calculation made by the causeless non-Buddhist outsiders (*nirhetuka-tīrthika*) of the West. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states:
"By what causes and conditions do those various non-Buddhists give rise to such views and establish such doctrines? The answer is: "Because they perceive that the world has no cause."
Due to these conditions: at times, a great wind may suddenly arise and in an instant become utterly still;
at times, a violent river may suddenly overflow and in an instant be completely dried up;
at times, flowers and trees may luxuriantly flourish and in an instant wither away. Because of such occurrences, the view of causelessness arises.
He established the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*). Qingliang remarked that this is largely similar to what is conceived by the Confucians and Daoists of this land.

Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the naked ascetic (Nagna) Brahmin sought to debate with the Buddha. The Buddha asked him, "For what reason does your school know that [things] are not produced by causes and conditions?
He replied, "I see that as soon as a cow is born, it can suckle milk; as soon as a tortoise is born, it can enter the water. Thus he knew.

"It is not due to causes and conditions. The Buddha said, "If you say that sucking milk is not due to causes and conditions, then neither [sucking milk nor sucking from a horn] would be due to causes and conditions;
why then do you not suck from a horn? If you say that entering water is not due to causes and conditions, then neither would be due to causes and conditions; why then do you not enter fire?
The Brahmin was speechless and, having surrendered to the Buddha, left the household life to become a monk.

Furthermore, birth would have no sequence of before or after; arising would have no distinction of early or late. Immortals would not depend on elixirs; the Great Peace would not depend on worthy and virtuous men;
benevolence and righteousness would not depend on instruction and practice.

Since it is said to be "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*), it should not depend on conditioning or practice. However, there are distinctions of time regarding priority, sequence, and timing; time is but one factor among remote conditions.
For example, the orchid in spring and the chrysanthemum in autumn, or the swallow at the community festival and the wild goose as a guest—each follows its own season.
Humans must wait until the tenth month before they are born; this is not spontaneous. From the immortals downward, we distinguish beings based on their sentient nature. As for the spirit...

A transcendent must possess the innate disposition of few desires from birth; only by taking the refinement of elixirs and the practice of *qi* as their causal conditions can they achieve longevity and freedom from aging.
For the world to be at peace, it must rely upon loyal ministers and virtuous scholars: arms to settle disorder and literature to govern the age.

When ruler and minister assist one another, the people will find security and the state will enjoy prosperity; seasons will be harmonious, customs pure, and individuals endowed with talent and virtue.
These excellences all rely on the power of instruction and admonition. Habit and nature are formed together; there has never been anyone who achieved self-perfection without learning.
To insist upon "natural spontaneity" (ziran) is it not a contradiction?
As for Laozi, Zhuangzi, Confucius, and Kongzi, what purpose did they have in establishing teachings as standards?

If the wise are naturally wise and do not arise from instruction and practice, and if the foolish are naturally foolish such that teaching is of no benefit, then the sages’ establishment of teachings would be rendered useless. Yet, in Laozi’s [distinction between] the superior person and the inferior person...

Regarding the Confucian Sage’s discourse on the "superior wisdom of the high" and the "inferior folly of the low," within our own teaching, this is generally due to the power of past habituation (*vāsanā*).

That is to say, because the cultivation of [wholesome] tendencies over many lifetimes has reached full maturity, one now attains human birth with all faculties sharp and keen; upon hearing the Way, one practices it with diligence.
In this regard, Confucius and Laozi are termed "superior men of innate knowledge" (*jñeyajña*). Thus, Bai Juyi was able to recognize characters from birth, which the world calls...

They are those who have been born as humans for three lifetimes. If, in past lives, they came from among other species and have never undergone spiritual cultivation, or perhaps due to secretiveness and stinginess they were unwilling to teach others, then having now obtained a human body, their faculties are dark and dull; they are vacant, ignorant, and muddled, remaining in distress yet refusing to study.
Confucius and Laozi referred to such people as the "lowest of the foolish" and the "lowest of the scholars. As for those of middling capacity, although they previously...
Although [the seeds] have been perfumed, they are not yet fully matured; therefore, in this present life, success is achieved through study, while failure looms in its absence.

Viewed from this perspective, even those of dull and inferior capacity, provided they can exert themselves in study, will—though perhaps not yet equal to those who have attained supreme realization—[attain their goal].

One surpasses those who do not study; how much more so does one surpass those of mediocre capacity? The Sage knew that learning and inquiry are beneficial, as they can transform ignorance into wisdom;
thus, he bequeathed the canonical instructions to serve as a standard and model. This clearly demonstrates the principle of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
To claim instead that things arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*) is surely not a sound reasoning.
Furthermore, as for the claim that "all things are generated from the primal qi (yuanqi)," this is a refutation established by examining the "primal qi" asserted by non-Buddhist schools.
If the spirit were produced spontaneously (*kṣubha*), having never undergone training or reflection, how could an infant be capable of such likes and dislikes, pride, and indulgence?
A newborn infant possesses all eight consciousnesses; yet, when first encountering external objects, it does not yet know how to become stained by attachment.
As it gradually grows up, through the power of habitual conditioning, likes and dislikes flourish and manifest. This is what is meant by "habit becomes one's nature";
it is not caused by the primal vital energy (*yuanqi*). *Xu* (欻) means to arise suddenly; it refers to arising abruptly.

If one were to say that things arise suddenly and can naturally follow one's thoughts—such as love, hatred, and so forth—then the five virtues and the six arts would all be understood by merely following one's thoughts;
why then would they need to be accomplished through the learning of causes and conditions?

Suppose it is said that when a child is first born, they are able to suckle at the breast and cry if they do not obtain it; surely this does not require prior cultivation or deliberation (*abhyāsa-vicāra*).

If so, why could they not naturally and spontaneously follow their thoughts regarding likes and dislikes, and likewise understand the five virtues and the six arts without depending on cultivation and deliberation?
Why is it not so? However, the fact that a human being knows how to drink milk and wail upon birth is due to beginninglessness (*anādi*).
Since ancient times, due to the power of habitual practice, these have arisen together with the mind. As previously stated, the ox does not bite with its horns and the tortoise does not enter fire;
both are matters of causes and conditions. How could it be that the primal qi (yuanqi) causes them to be so?
The five virtues are benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness. The six arts are ritual, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and mathematics.

Furthermore, if birth were merely the sudden presence of one who has received vital energy (*qi*), and death were the sudden absence resulting from the dispersal of that energy, then who would be the ghosts and spirits?
Confucianists all maintain that birth is the aggregation of *qi* and death is its dispersal. Now, if the *qi* disperses, it is simply annihilated.
Furthermore, who are ghosts and spirits? Confucius said, "Revere ghosts and spirits, yet keep them at a distance. The *I Ching* says, "Refined qi forms things; the wandering soul constitutes change;

thus one knows the nature and circumstances of ghosts and spirits. This refers to the hundred惊 (startling manifestations) and the four limbs, which are formed by the conjoining of the vital essence of male and female;
hence it is said that "refined qi forms things. As for what is called "the wandering soul constitutes change," it refers to [the process of transformation].

This is precisely as explained in the Buddhist teachings regarding consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*): because it is devoid of material obstruction, it can travel spontaneously; hence it is called a "wandering soul" (*youhun*).

The meaning is that the wandering soul unites with vital essence (*jingqi*) to become a human being. While the vital essence perishes, the wandering soul does not perish, and thus becomes a ghost or spirit (*guishen*).
Thus, it is clear that the Confucian tradition acknowledges the existence of ghosts and spirits. As for the vital essence...
If they were dispersed, who would be there?

Furthermore, there are those in the world who possess insight into past lives and can recall former events; from this, one knows that the continuity of existence prior to birth does not arise suddenly through the mere reception of vital breath.
To know past events before one’s birth is to possess knowledge of past lives (*jātismara*). This is like Yang Hu’s recognition of the golden ring.

(Yang Hu of the Jin dynasty, style name Shuzi, once as a young child led his wet nurse to the hollow of a withered tree outside the gate of Li’s residence. He found a single golden ring there and said to the wet nurse, "This was hidden by my predecessor when he was a child of the Li family.")

"I was seven years old when I fell into a well and died" (this account appears in his original biography). Regarding Cui Xian’s ink mark at birth: (Cui Xian of the Tang dynasty; his father Rui served as a secretary to Li Baozhen, the Regional Commander of Ze and Lu.

There was an elderly guest named Lu Lao who frequented Ze and Lu; Rui always treated him with great kindness. At the end of his life, Lu Lao said to Rui: "I shall become a son to your family, using an ink mark beside the mouth as proof.

When Xian was born, it was indeed just as he had said. This appears in his original biography). Regarding Fang Guan’s discovery of a book within a pine tree: (Fang Guan of the Tang dynasty, courtesy name Cilü, served as the Magistrate of Tonglu during the Kaiyuan era. He once [associated] with the Daoist Xing He...)

When Li Pó passed through Xiàkǒu, he entered an abandoned temple and sat beneath an ancient pine tree. He had his attendants dig into the ground, where they discovered letters addressed to the Chan Master Yǒng by Lóu Shídé, which had been stored inside a jar.

Laughing, he said to Lǐ Guǎn, "Do you recall this? Thereupon, Lǐ Guǎn was struck with realization that he had been the Chan Master Yǒng in a previous life. (From the *Mínghuáng zá lù*). Sūn Dōngpō wrote in a poem: "With earnest care beneath the ancient pine, he carved open the letter from within the jar.

Táng Shào bit the dog before the lamp. (Regarding Táng Shào: During the Kāiyuán era, he served as a Palace Secretary (*jìshìzhōng*). He was on friendly terms with the Commandant Lǐ Mào, who lived across the street, and treated him with great generosity. His wife once admonished him, saying, "Do not befriend those of a different class. Táng Shào... [text continues]

He said, "This is not something you know. Later, while the Martial Arts were being demonstrated at Mount Li, Zhang Shao was serving as the Minister of Rites. When Emperor Xuan took up the drumstick and struck the drum, the battle had not yet reached its third round when Zhang Yue suddenly ordered Shao to finish his performance.

Shenwu became violently enraged and dragged Guo Yuanzhen, the Minister of War, down from his seat beneath the military banner, intending to execute him. Zhang Yue knelt and petitioned, saying that Yuanzhen had meritorious service for the state; thus, he was spared from death, but Zhang Shao was executed instead. One day prior to this, Shao had said to his wife:

'In my previous life, I was a woman of the Du family who married the son of the Wang family of Ba-ling. At the age of seventeen, while practicing acupuncture by lamplight, I fell into a deep sleep. A dog entered the room and bumped into an oil lamp, staining my clothes. I became angry and stabbed the dog with a pair of scissors; one of its legs was severed, but the dog—'"

He remained alive. They replaced one of his ribs, and only then did the dog die; I was nineteen when I passed away. The dog is the one with this appearance today. The execution was set for the following day, and indeed on the next day it happened exactly as he had said:

the first blow did not sever the head, so they replaced the blade, and only then did the head fall. (Recorded by Li Jifu). Regarding Yuan Guan’s old appointment at Xiazhong: Tang dynasty, Li Chengzhi, styled Ziyuan, was a close friend of the Daoist Yuan Guan.

They made an agreement to travel from the Gorges into Shu together. On the road, they encountered a woman washing sand; Guan said to Yuan, "This is the place where I shall entrust my body. For karmic conditions cannot be escaped. "Next year, on such-and-such a day, you may come to visit me when you return from Shu."

He took a single smile as a sign of recognition. He further said, "I have already been a bhikṣu for three lifetimes," and so forth. Later, when Guǎn was about to die, the following year Yuán arrived at the girl’s house exactly as promised; the boy had already been born for three days. Yuán had the child held up near a bright eaves, and the boy indeed smiled.

Thirteen years later, Yuán went to Gūshān under the moonlight and heard someone tapping a cow horn and singing: "Upon the Stone of Three Lifetimes, our old spirits dwell; Whether we praise the moon or chant in the wind, let us not debate it.

How ashamed I am that my lover has come from afar to visit; Though this body differs, its nature remains ever-present. (Sū Dōngpō composed a biography of him. Sū Zīyóu dreamed of traveling to Shǎnyòu while in exile in Nán'ān.

He was a close associate of Yun’an and Chan Master Cong. One night, Yun’an dreamed that he, along with Ziyou and Master Cong, went out of the city to welcome Chan Master Wuzu Jie. The next morning, he told this dream to Ziyou; before he had finished speaking, Master Cong arrived and related his own dream exactly as Yun’an had described it.

While the mountain man was still laughing and chatting, a letter from东坡 (Sudō, Sūn Dāopó) suddenly arrived, saying: "I have already reached Fengxin; we shall meet within a day or two. The three men were overjoyed and together traveled twenty li out of the city to Jian’ansi, where Sudō also arrived. They recounted the dream to him, and Sudō said:

"When I was seven or eight years old, I once dreamed that I had become a monk and was traveling back and forth through Shǎnyòu. Furthermore, when my late mother was pregnant with me, she dreamed of a monk seeking lodging."

He was tall and slender, with one eye missing. Yun’an was startled and said, "Master Jie was a man from Shaanxi. Later he lost an eye, and in his later years he left Wuzu to travel to Nan’an, where he passed away at Dayu.

Counting back fifty years, this was when Su Dongpo was forty-nine. (From *Lengzhai Yehua*). Regarding the girl of Lu who remembered her past grievance over the sale of sheep: A woman from the house of Lu Shulun south of the city wall of Chang’an encountered a monk begging for food between the mulberry trees.

When asked where she could obtain a meal, the woman replied, "Two li east of the village, at the Wang family’s house, they provide a meal for monks. She went there and indeed received alms. When the Wang family asked the monk where he had come from, the monk told them the truth. Shortly thereafter, the Wang couple both arrived at the woman...

At home, the daughter did not come out, having closed the door. Her mother asked her, "A vegetarian feast has been prepared at my house, yet no one knows of it. How is it that you know? The daughter emerged from her room and called out, "On such and such a day and month, where are the father and son of the foreigner who sells sheep?"

The old man and woman rushed out in alarm. The mother asked her daughter, "What was that you were doing just now? The daughter replied, "In a previous life, I was a guest from Xiazhou who traded in sheep; my surname was Hu.

I stayed at their house, and they killed both my father and me, taking possession of all our sheep. Later, I was reborn as their son. At fifteen, I fell ill, and at twenty, I died. Although the expenses for medicine and treatment already exceeded what I had stolen, they still perform a vegetarian feast for me every year. Nevertheless, the debt of my life must still be repaid.

(From *Yishi*) **Resolving the Doubtful Case of Patricide in Xishan:** (At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Lizong of the Song dynasty, while Zhen Xishan was serving as the Military Commissioner of Changsha, there was a citizen named Cheng Erzhe whose son, aged twenty, plotted [to kill his parents].)

He murdered his father and spoke in secret to a friend. Fearing that the matter would be exposed and implicate him, the friend went to the authorities and confessed. The authorities immediately summoned the son and questioned him; he did not deny it. When they questioned the father and the neighbors, none knew how it had happened.

When they asked the son the reason for his patricide, there was nothing more he could say. Zhen examined the case and found it obscure, so he purified himself by ritual bathing and prayed to the deity. One night, he dreamed that the deity informed him: "Simply ask your father what he did twenty years ago, and you will know at once.

The next day, Zhen privately asked his father, "I already know this matter. You need only not deny it. What did you do twenty years ago? His father replied, "Twenty years ago, there was a practitioner from Mount Gui [Weishan]."

He took one thousand strings of cash with the intent of purchasing a *du-jiè* (ordination certificate). In the middle of the night, he killed a monastic and buried him beneath the kitchen, using that money to establish a business enterprise. Zhen later privately questioned his son: "I wish to let you go as a monk;

I would like to give you one thousand strings of cash so that you may go wherever you please. Once you have received this money, what will you do? The son replied, "If it is truly as you say, I shall purchase a *du-jiè* and enter Mount Wei to become a monk.

Zhen, realizing the monastic was his father’s enemy, subsequently registered his father’s estate and calculated its value at one thousand strings of cash, which he gave to his son. He then sent his father to a place five hundred *li* away. (From the *Jianghu Jiwen*). Instances such as these are indeed found throughout ancient and modern times.
Much. From this evidence, we know that when one body is cast off and another is received, there is a continuity of the same kind; it is not merely a matter of inheriting vital breath (*qi*).

Furthermore, since the spiritual cognition of ghosts and spirits is proven to be uninterrupted, we know that after death, it is not the case that the breath disperses and vanishes abruptly into nothingness.
Ghosts and spirits possess consciousness; this proves that there is no annihilation. If one were to claim that the vital breath disperses upon death, then who would be the "spirit"?
Therefore, the classics contain records of performing sacrifices and seeking prayers.

There are textual accounts in the classics; for instance, in the "Jintong" (The Golden Casket) chapter of the *Shangshu*, it is recorded that when King Wu was ill, the Duke of Zhou composed a memorial to pray to Kings Tai, Ji, and Wen, requesting to take their place.
He then placed the memorial within a casket sealed with golden cords (*jintong*). The following day, the King recovered.

Furthermore, there are accounts in the *Liji* (Book of Rites), specifically in the "Jifa" (Methods of Sacrifice), "Jiyi" (Meaning of Sacrifice), and "Jitong" (Principles of Sacrifice). Regarding the rites...
The *Yun* (Book of Rites) all speaks of matters concerning sacrifices and prayers. Furthermore, the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) states:

"He orders the officials to gather fodder to nourish the sacrificial animals, to provide for the Sovereign Heaven, the Supreme Deity, the spirits of the famous mountains and great rivers, and the deities of the four quarters;
to sacrifice to the numinous powers of the ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain, and to pray for blessings on behalf of the people. Such are its texts.

How much more so for those who have died and returned to life, recounting the affairs of the dark path, or who, after death, move their wives and children to seek retribution for enmity or repay kindness—
such things have occurred throughout both ancient and modern times, have they not?

The accounts concerning the dark paths of the afterlife are largely derived from Buddhist scriptures; fearing that Confucian scholars may not yet believe them, I shall now cite a statement by a Confucian to provide proof.
Ge Liping (style name Changzhi), Director of the Ministry of Personnel during the Song dynasty, wrote in his *Yunyuyangqiu*:
"Ouyang Yongshu was originally skeptical of the teachings of Śākyamuni. Once he had ascended to the two government offices..."

One day, while suffering from a critical illness, he dreamed that he arrived at a certain place where ten men wearing ceremonial caps and robes were seated in a circle. One man said, "Minister, how have you come to this?
You ought to return to your residence immediately. The official stepped out the door for several paces, then went back to ask him again:
"Are you not, sirs, what the followers of Śākya call the Ten Kings? They replied, "Indeed.

He then asked the men of the world, "Is it truly beneficial to provide meals for the monastic community and commission the production of scriptures to cultivate merit on behalf of the deceased? They answered, "How could it not be beneficial? Upon waking, [he realized this].
His illness was thoroughly cured. Furthermore, there is the case of Cui Ziyu presiding over the affairs of the underworld, and Han Qintu serving as King Yama (as recorded in the *Sou Shen Ji*).
There is also the case of Grand Preceptor Yu becoming the Buddha of Rebirth, and Prime Minister Xi becoming the Spirit of Pichang (as recorded in Hong Mai’s *Yijian Zhi*).
These are all proofs of events occurring in the netherworld (I cannot cite them all here). As for the words that moved even his wife and children and his enemies:
Regarding those who requite both enmity and gratitude, as recorded in the *Zuo Zhuan*, the fifteenth year of Duke Xuan: the Jin minister Wei Ke’s father, Wu Zi, had a favorite concubine.
When Wu Zi fell ill, he said to Ke, “You must marry her off. Later, when his illness became critical, he instead commanded that she be buried with him.
After Wu Zi died, Ke married her off, though his kinsmen opposed this. Ke replied, “I am following my father’s final testament. Subsequently—
Gao fought with the Qin general Du Hui at Fushi. He saw an old man binding grass to obstruct Du Hui;
[the general] stumbled and fell, and Gao captured him. That night, he dreamed of the old man, who said, "I am the father of the woman you married."
"You have fulfilled the dying command of your ancestors; it is for this reason that I have come to report to you. Furthermore, in the tenth year of Duke Cheng’s reign, Lord Jing of Jin fell ill.
He dreamed of a great malevolent spirit with disheveled hair reaching the ground, who beat her breast and leaped about, saying:

"To kill my descendants is unrighteous (two years prior, Lord Jing had executed his ministers Zhao Tong and Zhao Kuo without cause). I have obtained a petition from the Emperor" (the mention of the "Emperor" here likely refers to either the Emperor of the Five Peaks or the King of the Netherworld, as the matter concerns the realm of the unseen).

On the *bingwu* day of the sixth month, the Duke passed away. Furthermore, the *Jianghu Jiwen* records that the younger son of Zheng Chaoyi, a man of Quzhou during the Southern Song, was from childhood旷达 (vast and unencumbered) and capable in literature. He married a daughter of the Lu family of Kuaiji;
she too was graceful, charming, and bright. Their conjugal affection was profound. Zheng once said to the lady of the Lu family: "If, by some misfortune, [I should die], you must not..."
Regarding remarriage: "If you were to die first, I would do the same. Lu Shi said, "We ought to be 'eyebrow-to-eyebrow' (equal partners); how can such inauspiciousness be allowed?
They lived together for ten years and had two sons and one daughter. When Zheng fell ill and was on the verge of death, she only then removed her mourning garments.
Lu Shi took all his assets and went to Suzhou to marry into the family of Lord Zeng Cao; the marriage ceremony was completed just seven days later.
Once, while serving a transport commission to examine candidates in another district, Zeng Sheng traveled for two nights.

One evening, as Lu Shi was walking by the side of the administrative hall, a messenger hurriedly called out from the courtyard, saying, "Master Zheng has a letter. She ordered a maid to fetch it; upon seeing the outer title, she read: "To the Lady of the Lu Family."
There were only three characters left for the Lu family, their calligraphy appearing exactly like the handwriting of her late husband.
When she looked at the courier, he was already gone. Opening the seal and reading it, the words said: "For ten years we have been husband and wife with our hair tied together;
