for a lifetime you have been the master of our sacrifices. Morning and evening we shared joy together, and when our stipends had a surplus, we gathered as one. Suddenly, through a great illusion..."
Departing forever, for whom do you harbor such longing that you so lightly grant your consent? You have abandoned my fields and meadows;
you have shifted our assets and established a separate household. You show no pity for me having children, nor do you take thought for me having a father.

Your righteousness is insufficient to make you a wife to another, and your compassion is insufficient to make you a mother to another. I shall appeal this to the High Heaven; let your conduct be judged before the unseen spirits.
Lord Lu sighed in lamentation and died three days later. His son, Chao-yi Nan Dian, obtained his writings.
An external objection states: "If people become ghosts after death, then the ghosts from antiquity would fill the streets and alleys;
there ought to be those who see them. Why is this not so?"
This is a formal objection. When followers of external schools hear it said that when a person dies they become a ghost, they claim that every person, once dead, inevitably becomes a ghost.
Not knowing of the six realms of rebirth (*ṣaḍ-gati*) and the cycle of transmigration through successive bodies, they raise this objection.

The answer is: When humans die, they go to the six realms; it is not necessarily the case that all become ghosts. Ghosts, in turn, may become humans and so forth—how could it be that ghosts have existed as a constant accumulation since antiquity?
This is the response provided. As for "humans die and go to the six realms," it means that some may be born in heaven, some may return to being humans, or [others may go elsewhere].
They become birds or livestock, or they fall into the hells. As for what was previously called "ghosts," this refers merely to one realm of existence (*gati*).
Regarding the statement that ghosts may again become humans: this means that once their karmic retribution as ghosts is exhausted, they either become humans or transmigrate into other realms.

An example of such transmigration into another realm is recounted in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) of the Liang dynasty concerning the śramaṇa An Shigao during the Jianhe era of the Later Han dynasty.
As the boat traveled to Qiugong Lake, they moored there. On the bank stood a shrine to the lake deity.
The deity descended and said, "The śramaṇa on board was my spiritual companion in a previous life; please invite him for me.
An arrived at the shrine, and the deity wept as he pleaded, "I and you were once fellow practitioners of the Way. Because of a heart of anger, I fell into this realm. I pray that you..."
[He] took pity on [the creature] and sought to save it. The Master requested that the spirit manifest its true form. The spirit said, "My true form is hideous;
I fear you will be terrified. Dao'an replied, "Have no such concern. Suddenly, a large python emerged from behind the spirit and extended its head toward Dao'an.

Dao'an comforted it and preached the Dharma to transform and guide it using the language of India. The python wept and thanked him, saying, "Fortunately, I have heard your teaching; I am now liberated from suffering. Thus...
He bestowed one thousand bolts of silk and funds of yellow and white [currency] upon Dao’an, instructing him to perform meritorious deeds on their behalf.

Dao’an subsequently established a monastery in Yuzhang (the *Yeyu* states: this is the present-day Da’an Temple in Hongzhou). Shortly thereafter, he saw a large python lying dead in the marshes behind the mountain.
From that time on, the temple no longer manifested spiritual efficacy. This, too, is an example of a spirit’s transition through rebirth within the realms of existence.
Yet today, ignorant commoners go so far as to falsely claim that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the same as ghosts and spirits; their delusion and error are profound indeed!
Alas, how lamentable!
Furthermore, the qi of heaven and earth is fundamentally without consciousness. Humans receive this unconscious qi; how could it suddenly arise and possess consciousness?
Qi has no discrimination;
how could humans, by receiving it, come to possess discrimination? If humans, by virtue of receiving this qi...
If there were such differentiation, then even grasses, trees, and the like should possess it, for that which they receive is the same.
Furthermore, the qi of heaven and earth originally possesses no distinction between the worthy and the foolish, or the noble and the base;

how could it be that humans, while receiving this same qi, exhibit such distinctions of worthiness, folly, nobility, and baseness? Yet Confucianists all maintain that [distinctions arise from] the reception of qi, asserting that one receives pure and harmonious qi.
Thus, those who receive the pure and clear qi become sages and worthies, while those who receive the turbid qi become fools and unworthy.

One should not think that the qi of heaven and earth inherently possesses any distinction; rather, it is simply due to the differences in the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of each person from previous lives. This is like the sound of flutes and pipes:
as the air passes through different apertures, distinct notes are produced, resulting in variations of clarity and turbidity, or high and low pitches. Yet, as for the one who blows...
As for "qi," how could it ever be different? If you claim that there is a difference in the blowing of the breath, then why rely on the distinct apertures of bamboo flutes?
Furthermore, as for the white peaches and red apricots, or the Yao-huang and Wei-zǐ roses—could these not be the various differences produced by the spring breeze?
Why do you fail to examine the inherent nature of these things and instead place the blame upon the qi?
Plants and trees also all receive the vital breath (*qi*). Why do they not possess consciousness?
To raise this as an objection by way of example: one should also say that birds and beasts likewise all receive the vital breath; why then are their modes of flight and running different?
The qi of heaven and earth is like that of a furnace, a forge, a steamer, or a stove; it can only bring things to completion, but it is not the fundamental essence of the things themselves.
Thus, although a furnace or a forge can mold metal, they cannot transform copper or iron into fine ingots.

Although a steamer or a stove can cook food, they cannot transform chaff and husks into delicacies. So too, although the qi of heaven and earth can bring things to completion, [it does not constitute their ultimate nature].

One cannot cause grass and trees to become human, nor can the vulgar and ignorant become sages; this is simply because grass and trees each have their own roots, and humans and animals each have their own origins.

Furthermore, as for the claim that poverty or wealth, nobility or meanness, worthiness or folly, goodness or evil, and fortune or misfortune, calamity or blessing—all arise from the mandate of Heaven—this is likewise so.
This, moreover, establishes a refutation by examining the doctrine of "Heavenly Mandate" (tianming) held by non-Buddhist schools. Confucianists largely adhere to this concept of the Heavenly Mandate;
as earlier scholars explained, "Mandate" (ming) is synonymous with "command" (ling). In their school, they simply define Heaven as the pure qi that ascends to the highest, unsurpassed state.
If Heaven’s allotment of destiny were thus, why would there be so much poverty and so little wealth, so much lowliness and so little nobility, and even so much calamity and so little fortune?
If such disparities as these were determined by Heaven, why is Heaven not impartial?

The Way of Heaven is supremely impartial and level; it is without bias and without factionalism. For what reason, then, do there exist such differences as poverty and wealth, nobility and meanness, wisdom and folly, misfortune and fortune, and the abundance or scarcity of blessings?
Furthermore, among these, those who are poor, lowly, unfortunate, or short-lived are many, while those who are wealthy, noble, healthy, or long-lived are few.
This is witnessed by all in the ways of the world, occurring constantly in this manner. If Heaven were truly thus, then it would be fair and even.
Where does this lie?

How can it be that those who practice nothing are honored, while those who maintain their conduct are held in contempt; that those without virtue are wealthy, while those with virtue are poor; that the contrary is auspicious and the righteous are calamitous;
that the benevolent die young and the violent live long; and even that those who possess the Way perish, while those who lack the Way flourish?
To be noble without practicing virtue is like what Xunzi calls "the glory of power. To be base while maintaining one's conduct is like Ren Fang’s claim to his own "plain integrity.
To be wealthy without merit is like He Zhao, who reportedly consumed ten thousand coins daily. To be poor despite possessing virtue is like Sima Xiangru, whose home had nothing but four walls.
To have misfortune despite being upright and good fortune despite being wicked is like when the treacherous and corrupt achieve their ambitions while the virtuous and kind meet with calamity.

Regarding the category of those who suffer harm: there are cases where the benevolent meet an early end while the violent enjoy longevity, such as the case of Robber Zhi (Dào Zhí) living to an old age while Bó Ní died young.

As for the distinction between those with the Way and those without it, we see that even the virtuous of this world often encounter setbacks and misfortunes at every turn, whereas the arrogant, aggressive, and greedy frequently find success and advantage in all their dealings.
From antiquity to the present day, such instances have always existed. The common people often claim that Heaven is unjust, or—
It is said that when Heaven does not open its eyes, Deng You was left without sons; this is what people mean when they say "Heaven knows nothing.
Since all things depend on Heaven, yet Heaven promotes the unrighteous and destroys the righteous, how can there be blessings for those who do good, or benefits for those who are humble?
Rewards are the punishments for those who indulge in depravity and those who are overfilled with arrogance.
The Confucian masters hold fast to the mandate of Heaven, yet they do not realize that they themselves contradict this teaching. The *Book of Documents* says:

"The Way of Heaven blesses the good and brings calamity to the depraved. The "Yi Xun" chapter says: "For performing good, it sends down a hundred auspicious signs; for performing evil, it sends down a hundred calamities. (From the *Hong Fan* chapter.)
Heaven employs the five blessings; Earth employs the six extremities. The *Qian* hexagram of the *Yi Jing* states: "The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the humble.
The Way of Earth transforms the full and flows toward the humble. Ghosts and spirits harm the full and bless the humble. The *Kun* hexagram states:

"A family that accumulates goodness will surely have an abundance of auspiciousness; a family that accumulates evil will surely have an abundance of calamity. In essence, all these passages refer to this.

The Way of Heaven is manifest; its retribution of calamity and fortune is never errant. Yet now we see the unrighteous flourish while the righteous perish, which seems to suggest that the teachings of the *Book of Changes* and other classics lack verification.
Furthermore, when the virtuous and good meet with harm, the rewards for "blessing the good" and "honoring humility" are utterly subverted;
when the wicked and depraved attain their ambitions, the punishments for "visiting calamity upon the licentious" and "harming the overfull" are turned upside down. Examining these texts...

Examining the facts, they are entirely inconsistent; thus, one asks how this could be so. This is truly because one fails to investigate the principles of karma and merely clings to the doctrine of fate;
consequently, misfortune and fortune are sometimes inverted.

Furthermore, if calamities, rebellions, and acts of defiance all arise from the mandate of Heaven (tian-ming), then it would be improper for sages to establish teachings that hold people accountable rather than Heaven, or blame things rather than the mandate. This would be unjust.
When people of the world hear accounts of the chaos and order of antiquity and the present, there are none who do not attribute it all to the decrees of Heaven (*tian-shu*).

If these matters were determined by Heaven, then what the scriptures teach should only hold Heaven accountable; why then do they hold only humans responsible? This is as criticized in the *Shi* and *Shu*.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* censures [transgressions], yet it does not criticize or condemn the mandate of Heaven;

why is this so? If that were the case, then the *Odes* would be merely criticizing chaotic governance, the *Book of Documents* would be praising the Way of the King, the *Rites* would be extolling the pacification of superiors, and the *Music* would be titled for shifting customs—how could these possibly be considered acts of serving the will of High Heaven or following the mind of the Creator?

Since it is said that fortune and calamity arise from Heaven and do not depend on human effort, and since Heaven is the principle of spontaneity that admits neither increase nor decrease, then are the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music—which punish evil and encourage goodness, leading people to avoid calamity and pursue fortune so as to receive Heaven’s blessings—not empty words?
The Odes consist of the *Guofeng*, *Yaya*, and *Song*; regarding good, they are beautiful, and regarding evil, [they are]...

The *Shu* (Book of Documents) contains various forms of writing—canons, prolegomena, instructions, admonitions, oaths, and mandates—all of which clarify the Way of the Two Emperors and Three Kings for governing the world and transforming the people.
The *Xiaojing* says: "To bring peace to superiors and to govern the people, nothing is better than ritual (*li*). It transforms customs and changes social mores."
Nothing is more beneficial than music. All these works—the Odes, the Documents, the Rites, and the Music—are intended to guide the human heart toward the path of goodness.
To rely on human effort to usurp the authority of the Creator—how could this possibly be to serve the will of Heaven or accord with the mind of Heaven?
It is simply that the scholars of the world do not understand that the source of spiritual resonance lies within themselves; they have consistently attributed it [to external forces].
The doctrine of "Heaven’s Mandate" not only contradicts the Buddhist teaching on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), but also violates the fundamental intent of one's own school’s *Shi*,
*Shu*, *Li*, and *Yue*. Thus,
we know that those who adhere exclusively to this teaching have failed to investigate the nature of man.
This concludes the preceding discussion on the incomplete meanings (*neyārtha*) of the non-Buddhist traditions of Confucianism and Daoism.
Second, the refutation of partiality and shallowness (referring to those who practice the incomplete teachings of Buddhism).

Within Buddhism, there are five general levels of teaching, ranging from the shallow to the profound: first, the Teaching for Humans and Devas; second, the Teaching of the Hīnayāna; third, the Great [Vehicle]... [text fragment ends].

The Teaching on the Characteristics of the Vehicle of Multiplicity; the Teaching on the Destruction of Characteristics of the Four Mahāyānas (the former four are contained within this fascicle); and fifth, the Teaching on the Manifestation of Nature of the One Vehicle (contained within the third fascicle).

These five types of teaching were categorized by Guifeng according to their underlying meaning. Because there are five distinct capacities among those to be taught (the *yāna*), there are consequently these five types of teaching that can reach them.
As for the "five vehicles" (*pañca-yāna*): first, the vehicle of humans and devas; second, the vehicle of the śrāvakas;

third, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas; fourth, the vehicle of the bodhisattvas; and fifth, the Buddha-vehicle. (This is based on the meaning of the second stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the "Chapter of Maitreya" from the *Awakening of Faith*). From...
The dharmas sought are merely designated by the name of "vehicles" (*yāna*). Now, by combining the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* and opening up the *bodhisattva*, these five are established.

If one explains the five kinds of spiritual lineages (*gotra*) according to the Dharma-characteristics school (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), they are: first, the lineage of the *śrāvaka* vehicle; second, the lineage of the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle;
third, the lineage of the *bodhisattva* vehicle; fourth, the indeterminate lineage; and fifth, the absence of lineage (*agotra*). Within the category of the indeterminate...
Furthermore, there are four categories: first, the *śrāvaka* and bodhisattva lineage; second, the *pratyekabuddha* and bodhisattva lineage; third, the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* lineage;
and fourth, the *śrāvaka*, *pratyekabuddha*, and bodhisattva lineage. Those who lack a lineage (*agotra*) refer to those who entirely lack the seeds of the aforementioned three vehicles.
Now, the teachings for humans and devas include those without a lineage, while the Hīnayāna teachings include those of the *śrāvaka* lineage.
The two natures of the Pratyekabuddhas are subsumed within the latter three teachings. The indeterminate nature is encompassed by the middle three teachings.
According to Xianshou’s Five Teachings, the first—the Hinayana Teaching—corresponds to this second [teaching]. The second—the Initial Mahayana Teaching—corresponds to the third and fourth.
The third is the Final Teaching; the fourth is the Sudden Teaching; and the fifth is the Perfect Teaching, which corresponds to this [present teaching].
Fifth, because the latter three [teachings] of Xianshou are all based upon the One Vehicle, Guifeng combined them.
Xianshou distinguished between the common and distinct teachings, opening up three variations regarding the presence or absence of sequential stages.

However, his "Initial Teaching" (shijiao) subsumes both the Indian schools of Emptiness and Characteristics, as both fail to fully exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma; therefore, he combined them into the first [teaching]. (The first is...)

At the outset, Guifeng followed the Western Regions in maintaining two [categories], sometimes opening them and sometimes merging them; each has its own appropriate application and cannot be standardized by a single rule.
Master Wansong, within this treatise, establishes nine pairs and eighteen layers that comprehensively encompass the meanings of the two types of Five Teachings (Wujiao) of both Xianshou and Guifeng.
First, the pair of suffering and pleasure (taking the three miserable realms as opposed to humans and devas). Second, the pair of humans and devas.

1. The correspondence between man and heaven (taking man as the counterpart to heaven). 2. The correspondence between concentration and distraction (the desire realm is distraction; the two upper realms are concentration). 3. The correspondence between form and emptiness (viewing the four dhyānas in relation to the four formless attainments). 4. The correspondence between ordinary beings and sages (the first four are all ordinary beings;

the latter three vehicles are sages). 5. The correspondence between the Small and the Great (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are Small; from the Initial Teaching onward, they are all Great). 6. The correspondence between the beginning and the end (Dharmalakṣaṇa is the beginning; Dharmatā is the end). 7.

The correspondence between the sudden and the gradual (the beginning and end involve traversing stages; in the Sudden Teaching, these are not established). 8. The correspondence between the partial and the perfect (according to Xianshou, the first four [teachings] are...)

All [other schools] are partial, whereas the *Avataṃsaka* alone constitutes the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Thus, within Xianshou’s system of the Small Vehicle teachings, he skillfully opens up the first five pairs to encompass the doctrines of this treatise;
it may be said that his phrasing is concise while his principles are exhaustive.

A single Buddha, for the sake of beginners, first explains the karmic retribution of the three periods of time and the causes and effects of good and evil, clarifying the teachings of humans and devas.
Within this, he first states the general title and the essential meaning. "Beginners" refers to those who are the intended audience.

With respect to the latter three vehicles, it is called the "initial mind. Because it is exclusively a skillful means, it is said to be "merely explained. Regarding the karmic retribution of the three periods of time:
this refers to karma created in the past being experienced as retribution in the present life, and karma created in the present life being experienced as retribution in a future life.
Therefore, it is called the "three periods. Karma is the cause that brings about [retribution], and retribution is the fruit that is brought about.
Since both karma and retribution encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, they are termed the "causes and effects of good and evil," as will be explained in detail below.

This refers to committing the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) to a superior degree, whereby one falls into hell upon death; to a middling degree, one becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*); and to an inferior degree, one becomes an animal (*tiryagyoni*).

Having first described the causes and effects of evil, the "ten unwholesome actions" are defined as follows: three of the body—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—and four of speech—false speech, [malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter].
Divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; and the three of the mind: greed, hatred, and wrong view. Regarding the term "superior grade" (*uttama-pakṣa*):

generally speaking, both wholesome and unwholesome [actions] are each divided into three grades, which are clarified through three criteria. The first is in terms of the object (*viṣaya*). For example, regarding the taking of life:

killing a human being is superior; killing an animal is middling; killing a mosquito or gnat is inferior. The opposite applies to non-killing: refraining from killing a human being is considered inferior.

First, regarding the object: not killing even a mosquito is superior. Second, regarding the mind: setting aside whether it is virtuous or non-virtuous, acting with a fierce and intense mind is superior;

acting with a casual mind is inferior; and acting with a mediocre mind is intermediate. Third, regarding the time: whether virtuous or non-virtuous, if there is no regret for three periods [of time], it is superior;
if there is no regret for two periods, it is intermediate; and if only one period, it is inferior. As for the hells:

Regarding the term "etcetera" (*ādi*): in Sanskrit it is called *naraka*, which here means "vessel of suffering" (*duḥkha-bhājana*), referring to the vessel in which sentient beings undergo suffering.
What is now termed "hell" (*dīya-naraka*) is a name established based on its meaning. Some say that "earth" (*dīya*) means "bottom" (*tala*) and "prison" (*naraka*) means "confinement" (*niyata*).

Since there are prisons beneath the earth, they are called "earth-prisons" (*dīya-naraka*). In total, there are four categories: namely, the eight hot hells, the eight cold hells, the neighboring hells (*utsada-naraka*), and the isolated hells (*pratyeka-naraka*).
Regarding the term "the eight hot hells": the first is called Saṃjīva (Reviving). This means that one is cut and hacked into thousands of pieces with knives and swords;

these are gathered together and struck with forks, while the voice cries out, "Live! Live! Thereupon, one immediately revives. Having revived, one is hacked again; having been hacked, one revives once more.

Therefore, it is called "Equal Revival" (Saṃjīva). Taking five hundred years as the lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings—(the lifespans of the various heavens are detailed in the text below)—as one day and night, when such a count accumulates to five hundred years, it is [the first hell].
The second is called "Mass Crushing" (Kālasūtra), where four mountains close together and crush the bodies of the offenders until they are like fine dust;
taking one thousand years as the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as one day and night...
[The second hell] is called Saṃghāta (Crushing). Accumulating such days over months and years, their lifespan is one thousand years. The third is called Kālasūtra (Black Rope).

Just as wood is split in the world by being bound with ropes and sawn apart, [the beings here are likewise tortured]. Taking the two-thousand-year lifespan of the Yāma Heaven as one day and night, their lifespan is two thousand years.

The fourth is called Raurava (Howling). A day and night there is equal to four thousand years of the Tuṣita Heaven; their lifespan is four thousand years. The fifth is called Mahāraurava (Great Howling).
A day and night there is equal to eight thousand years of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; their lifespan is eight thousand years. The sixth is called Tapana (Scorching).
A day and night there is equal to sixteen thousand years of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. Their lifespan is... [sixteen thousand years].
The seventh is called Intense Heat (*Pratāpana*); its lifespan is half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
This refers to the period beginning when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, decreasing by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years;

this duration is termed a half-intermediate kalpa, which constitutes the lifespan of this hell. The eighth is Avīci, translated here as "Without Interval" (*Muzhuan*). It is established as such for five reasons.
There are four types of "immediacy" (ānantarya): first, immediacy of action, which is explained in terms of punishment;
second, immediacy of retribution, which is explained in terms of karmic fruition; third, immediacy of suffering, which is explained in terms of agony; and fourth, immediacy of lifespan.
Because there is no premature death. Fifth, as for "uninterrupted" (*avīci*): it refers to the physical dimensions being without interval.

That is to say, due to their own karma, sentient beings each perceive their bodies filling the hell with no empty space between them; therefore, it is called "uninterrupted. The lifespan in this hell is one *antara-kalpa* (intermediate kalpa) of increase and decrease.
Regarding the eight cold hells: the first is called Arbuda, which translates as "blister. The suffering of the cold touches the body like [a blister].

1. Arbuda (Blistering), so called because of blisters. 2. Nirarbuda (Bursting Blister), so called because the body freezes and cracks. (These two names are established based on the characteristic of suffering. 3. Aṭaṭa (Chattering Teeth), 4. Hahava (Lamentation), and 5. Huhuva (Moaning).
(These three names are established based on the bodies experiencing the suffering. 6. Utpala (Blue Lotus), 7. Padma (Red Lotus), and 8. Mahāpadma (Great Red Lotus).
(The bodies, touched by the suffering of cold, change color to these respective hues. Regarding the lifespan of these eight cold hells, there are two different explanations.
The same. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is even longer than the preceding. For example, the lifespan of the first Ābhāsvara devas is so vast that its number cannot be known.
The Buddha said it is like this: suppose there were twenty *droṇas* of sesame seeds in the kingdom of Kośala, filled to the brim and not leveled off.
If one were to remove a single seed every hundred years until these twenty *droṇas* of sesame seeds were exhausted, their lifespan would still not have ended.
This concludes the count. To calculate it roughly by these figures, the remaining seven hells increase in number by doubling each time.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the life spans in the eight cold hells are successively reduced by half compared to those in the eight hot hells;
for example, Arbuda is half the duration of Saṃjīva, and this continues until Mahāpadma, which is likewise half the duration of Avīci. Based on this...
Thus, these eight cold hells are lighter than the eight hot hells. Regarding the three neighboring hells: at each of the four gates of the eight hot hells, there are four such hells.

The first is called *Kukūla* (the Pit of Hot Ashes), where boiling ashes reach the knees; when one lowers the foot, it is scorched and rotted away, yet when the foot is lifted, it is restored as before.

The second is called *Kuṇapa* (the Pit of Corpse-Feces), where a mire of excrement reaches the knees and contains venomous insects that devour one’s flesh entirely upon lowering the foot. When the foot is lifted... [it is restored].
Third is the Path of Blades: the edges of swords, blades, and the like are spread out as a road; treading upon them causes one to be cut and wounded. Fourth is the River of Ashes:
boiling hot caustic ash, in which one is either boiled or stewed until the skin and flesh are decomposed and putrefied.

Regarding the four solitary hells (*ekāntika-naraka*), their locations are not fixed; they may be found among mountains, beneath trees, in wildernesses, at city walls, and so forth, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
It is said that they dwell in isolation on the outskirts [of the human realm] and their lifespans are indefinite, varying according to the length of their karma.

As for those called "hungry ghosts" (*preta*), it is because they endure hunger for a long time that they are termed "hungry ghosts. Their conditions vary in degree of severity, and there are generally nine classes.

The first is called the "torch-mouthed ghost," meaning that fierce flames constantly issue from their mouths. The second is the "needle-throated ghost," whose head and belly are as large as mountains, yet whose throats are [as narrow as needles].
1. The Needle-Throat Ghost: its throat is like a needle. 2. The Foul-Mouthed Ghost: its mouth is like a putrid corpse.

These three are called the "ghosts without wealth" because they are unable to obtain food. 4. The Great-Tumor Ghost: it has a tumor on its neck; it uses its hand to tear out the pus and eats it itself.
5. The Needle-Haired Ghost: the hair on its body is like needles; it pricks its own body with them, and eats the blood that flows out.
The sixth is the *Pūtimukha* (Foul-Smelling Hair) ghost. The hair on its body is foul and filthy; out of aversion, it plucks it out, takes the blood, and eats it.

These three are called the *Alpabhoga* (Little Wealth) ghosts, because they obtain little food and drink. The seventh is the *Ucchiṣṭa-bhuj* (Eater of Remnants) ghost, which constantly obtains the discarded food left over from sacrifices.
The eighth is the *Vighasa-bhuj* (Eater of Scraps) ghost, which constantly obtains the food dropped in the streets and alleys. The ninth is the *Iśvara*... [text truncated]
The *bala-rākṣasas* (power-ghosts) are of three kinds: first, yakṣas; second, rākṣasas; and third, piśācas.
These three names refer to those who possess much wealth, because they obtain abundant food and drink.
For these aforementioned ghosts, twenty human days constitute one day and night; they further reckon thirty such days as one month, and twelve months as [one year].
One year [of humans] is one day for them; their lifespan is five hundred years. This is based on the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Some say that the lifespan in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) is indefinite, with the longest being seventy thousand years. Regarding "animals" (*tiryag-yoni*): "animal" (*chu*) means "to nourish";

they are those nourished by humans, such as oxen, horses, dogs, and pigs. This definition is restrictive. Alternatively, they are called "those born sideways" (*tiryag-yoni*), meaning they are born moving horizontally; this applies universally.
This term encompasses all classes of flying and running creatures; thus, its scope is broad. To speak of them specifically, there are the feathered, the scaly, the shelled, and the armored;

the wriggling, the crawling, the flying, and the submerged—their varieties are numerous and vast. Among these, those with the greatest merit include the nāgas and the garuḍas, both of which undergo birth through all four modes.
However, the lifespan of beings in the animal realm is not fixed; at its longest, it lasts for one intermediate kalpa. Extensive.
As in the separate chapter (this is cited from Guifeng’s *Xingyuan Chao*). Regarding the current statement that the middle grade refers to hungry ghosts and the lower grade to animals:
Guifeng made this correlation based on treatises such as the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

However, according to the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, animals are considered the middle grade and hungry ghosts the lower. Qingliang cites the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* to clarify that although...
The three miserable realms each have both primary and secondary categories. The primary is considered heavy, while the secondary is considered light.

From the perspective of the primary ghosts relative to the secondary animals, the ghosts are heavy and the animals are light (as in the current text). From the perspective of the primary animals relative to the secondary ghosts, the animals are heavy and the ghosts are light (as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*).

Therefore, the Buddha provisionally modeled his teachings on the five constant virtues of the world (the worldly teachings of India; although their rituals differ, there is no distinction in their deterring evil and encouraging good, nor do they deviate from the five virtues such as benevolence and righteousness;
thus there are virtuous practices to be cultivated, similar to how in this country one raises the hands together while in Tibet one lets them hang loose—both are considered forms of propriety).
The following clarifies the causes and effects of wholesome karma. The five precepts, the ten wholesome actions, the four dhyānas, and the eight samādhis are the wholesome causes;

rebirth among humans, devas, and so forth, are the wholesome effects. Here, we first discuss the "Human Vehicle" (puruṣayāna). "Category" (lei) means to draw analogies; "worldly" (shi) refers to the secular world, encompassing both the Western Regions and this land [of China].

This does not refer merely to the Five Constant Virtues (wuchang) taught by the Duke of Zhou and Confucius. As for what are called the Five Constant Virtues, they are: benevolence (ren), righteousness (yi), propriety (li), wisdom (zhi), and faithfulness (xin).
Wisdom and faith are what people constantly practice; even in moments of haste or distress, one cannot be parted from them.

In the commentary, the two systems of worldly teachings are separately reconciled to demonstrate their great commonality, while also implicitly addressing potential objections. This is done for fear that people might doubt, saying: "The Buddha appeared in India;
the rituals and institutions of that country’s worldly teachings may differ [from ours]. Why then do you say they are similar to these Five Constant Virtues? They ought to—"
This is because Buddhism imitated Confucius and Laozi and thus fabricated these harmonizations; hence, he provides this explanation, etc.
Furthermore, Nāgārjuna’s *Mahāyānopadeśa-śāstra* cites the *Dàodǐng jīng* (a text not extant in this land) to establish four dharma-piṭakas:

first, the *pudgala-piṭaka*. (*Pudgala* here means "one who repeatedly takes up [existence]"; because one repeatedly creates karma and takes up rebirth in other realms, it refers specifically to human beings. The sutra says: "O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively..."

Listen as I explain them for you: the treasury of benevolence (*ren*), the treasury of righteousness (*yi*), the treasury of propriety (*li*), the treasury of wisdom (*zhi*), and the treasury of faith (*xin*)—these being the treasuries of humans and devas—as well as the treasury of the śrāvakas, the treasury of the bodhisattvas, and the treasury of the Dharma of the Great Awakened One. Why is this?
Because for all practitioners, there is a gradual progression toward excellence through the sequence of the Dharma.

As for "Tianzhu" (India): it refers to the region west of the Pamir Mountains. There are five regions of India, known as the Five Tianzhus. Because during the period of the formation of the eon (*kalpa*), beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended and were born there, they received the name of "Heaven. In Sanskrit, it is called *Āryadeśa* (Land of the Noble Ones), or alternatively *Śin-tu* (Body-Poison); these were corrupted and abbreviated to "Zhu."

Regarding what is called "worldly instruction," this refers to the teachings by which kings govern the world. In the Western Regions, wherever the Buddha-dharma exists, nations are governed according to the Dharma of the Buddha; as seen, for example, in the *Rājanīti-samyukta-parivarta* (Chapter on the Correct Treatise on Royal Law) within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*. Furthermore, Wheel-turning Kings transform the world through the ten wholesome paths of action, following the bequeathed teachings of the Buddhas of antiquity.

As for the statement that "ceremonial forms differ," this refers to such matters as the calendar, the first day of the year, and styles of dress and headwear, which vary according to region. Nevertheless, the punishment of evil and the encouragement of goodness are largely identical to those of this land [China].

Although virtuous practices are manifold, if one summarizes their great principles, they do not exceed the five constants—benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and sincerity—through which the principles of the world can be discerned. Ultimately, the correct truth converges into one; therefore, the methods for governing the world are like two halves of a tally that fit together perfectly. It is not that Zhou and Confucius alone created these models specifically for the people of this realm.
Nor did the Tathāgata establish his teachings by imitating this region.

He commanded that the five precepts be observed: not killing is benevolence; not stealing is righteousness; not committing sexual misconduct is propriety; not speaking falsely is faithfulness; and abstaining from drinking alcohol and eating meat keeps the spirit and breath pure, which benefits wisdom.

If one reverses the aforementioned ten unwholesome actions, they are collectively termed the "ten wholesome actions. In the second stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is taught that the ten wholesome actions encompass the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*):

namely, as a cause for those of inferior capacity; as a cause for the gods of middling capacity; as a cause for the three vehicles (*triyāna*) of superior capacity; and as a cause for Buddhahood of the highest-superior capacity.

Furthermore, within the framework of the monastic discipline (*vinaya*), the Buddha also established the five precepts for lay followers (*upāsaka*), which likewise encompass the five vehicles. Thus, we know that...

The five precepts and the ten wholesome actions are largely the same, differing only slightly; their expansion or contraction follows what is appropriate, much like the six perfections and ten perfections of the Mahāyāna.

(Note: The five precepts are correlated with the Five Constant Virtues because they share the same underlying meaning. Master Mingjiao said: "Abstaining from killing on a single day" means one should love living beings and not harm a single thing; it does not merely mean refraining from eating their meat. Mencius said: "To kill one... )

It is not a sin, yet it is not benevolence (*ren*). Therefore, non-killing is taken as benevolence. Second, regarding non-stealing: this means not taking what is not rightfully one's own; it does not merely refer to refraining from seizing the property of others.

As Mencius said: "To take what is not one's own is contrary to righteousness. Third, non-lust: this means not becoming disordered with those who are not one's proper match. Since ritual (*li*) is that by which suspicions are resolved, similarities and differences are distinguished, and right and wrong are clarified, one must likewise refrain from lust.

Fourth, non-lying: this means not deceiving others with one's words. Since the trustworthy person’s speech does not waver, one likewise refrains from falsehood. Fifth, non-drinking and non-eating: because of drinking and eating, the spirit and mind become turbid and chaotic, and the emotions and thoughts become deluded and frantic, thereby harming wisdom. Therefore, one does not consume excess food; this is so that intellectual thought may remain pure. However—

Regarding these five precepts within the context of the *vinaya* discipline, there are further distinctions between being complete or deficient in terms of their components (*aṅga*) and their duration (*kāla*). To be able to maintain all five precepts is termed "complete in components" (*aṅga-sampanna*). Alternatively, to be able to maintain only four, three, or two is termed "deficient in components" (*aṅga-vikala*). To maintain them for as long as one lives is termed "complete in duration" (*kāla-sampanna*).

Alternatively, to be able to maintain them for ten years, five years, or down to a single day, is termed "deficient in duration" (*kāla-vikala*). When comparing the components and the duration, there should be four possible permutations regarding completeness and deficiency. Based on this, there are lay followers (*upāsaka*) who are categorized as having one part, a small part, a large part, or the full part.

Among these five [precepts], because the precept against killing is deficient, although one obtains a human body, one suffers from many illnesses and a short lifespan. Because the precept against stealing is deficient, one lacks sufficient wealth and resources. Because the precept against sexual misconduct is deficient, one lacks excellent kinsmen and retinues. Because the precept against false speech...

Because it is absent, one says that no one experiences [the result]; because it is absent, one does not drink. The various faculties are dull and obscured. Furthermore, among these five, the first four are *prakṛti-śīla* (natural precepts); that is, killing, stealing, and so forth, whose very nature is sinful, and are thus called natural precepts. The single precept of drinking alcohol is a *pratikṣepaṇa-śīla* (prohibitory precept).
Because food and drink disturb one's nature and cause one to transgress the previous four, the Buddha established this [precept] to prevent those four; therefore, it is called a prohibitory precept.
One escapes the three miserable realms and is reborn among human beings.

Regarding the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, one receives them all from a teacher based upon the Three Refuges; at the moment the words are spoken, one obtains this essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*).

First one receives the Three Refuges, and subsequently the five precepts and the ten precepts. Because of taking refuge in the Buddha, one does not fall into hell; because of taking refuge in the Dharma, one does not...

One would have fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts; however, because one takes refuge in the Sangha, one does not fall into the animal realm and thus escapes the three miserable paths. This is due to the power of the Three Refuges.
There has never been anyone who attained the precepts without first taking refuge in the Triple Gem, for the reception of the five precepts must necessarily be preceded by the Three Refuges.
Therefore, they are omitted here.

By practicing the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) of the superior grade, as well as generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and so forth, one is reborn in the heavens of the six desire realms (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*). By practicing the four dhyānas and the eight meditative attainments (*aṣṭa-samāpatti*), one is reborn in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

(The reason the titles do not specify "heavens, ghosts, or hells" is that their realms and levels differ; what can be seen or heard does not reach them. If even ordinary people do not know the branches, how much less would they be willing to exhaustively investigate the root? Thus, this is addressed for the sake of the laity.)
[This is] the teaching. First, the original person is identified; now, the Buddhist scriptures are cited (it would be appropriate to list them in full).
Regarding the ten wholesome actions of the superior grade, there are two meanings. First, because they are "superior" in comparison to the preceding five precepts, they are called the superior grade.
Second, among humans, the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*) are considered inferior; therefore, those of the heavens are regarded as superior.

The ten wholesome actions of the heavens constitute the general category, while giving and the others are the specific instances. This means that when one cultivates the ten wholesome actions with a distracted mind, they are practiced concurrently with acts such as giving.
One is born in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). When accompanied by a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), one is born in the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*): killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are the same as the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*). Fifth is refraining from frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), which means not embellishing one's words to conceal faults.

Sixth is refraining from divisive speech (*paiśunya*), which means not speaking behind someone's back. Seventh is refraining from harsh speech (*pāruṣya*), meaning one’s words must always be kind and compliant. Eighth is refraining from covetousness (*abhidhyā*), which means the mind is constantly...
Being content with existence and the requisites for existence, one does not give rise to defiled attachment. Ninth is non-anger, which means not harboring resentment or malice in the heart.
Tenth is the absence of wrong views, which means that the mind and vision are upright, free from deception and flattery.
Regarding these latter six precepts, various teachings list them with minor variations; yet they do not contradict one another. Furthermore, there is a sutra in which they are combined.
The four verbal [precepts] are reduced to three: namely, not slandering (which encompasses both divisive speech and harsh speech), not deceiving (which is frivolous speech), and not lying.

(As for the names,) adding "not drinking alcohol" and "not eating meat" makes four. In the *Avataṃsaka*, among these four verbal precepts, false speech, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech are listed in that order;
this is according to their relative gravity. This is from Master Song’s *Fujiao bian* (Compendium on Assisting the Teachings).

The three mental factors are listed as greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). (Therefore, greed was explained previously; this is based specifically on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. The *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* apply exclusively to the Mahāyāna, so they do not coincide here.
However, regarding how these three mental factors can constitute paths of action (*karmapatha*), the Great Commentary by Qingliang, relying on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, states:

"If greed is not yet determinate, it is merely termed an affliction (*kleśa*; defilement); once it becomes determinate, it is termed an action (*karman*; path of action). This is likewise true for hatred and delusion."
Among the three types of intentional [karma], one must fulfill five conditions for it to constitute a full course of action (*karmapatha*).

These five conditions are: first, the object (referring generally to another's property, as it is possessed by another); second, the substance (the specific object of craving, such as gold, silver, wealth, or treasures); third, the distinction, which consists of three parts:

first, seeking (initial desire is called "seeking," which involves the perception that the object belongs to another); second, wishing (hoping to acquire it for oneself, which is the inclination or desire); and third, coveting (ultimately giving rise to the thought of seizing it, which constitutes greed). Regarding these...

Within the distinctions, the first two are the preparatory means (*upāya*) and the last one is the culmination (*niṣṭhā*). Together with the preceding essential entity, these constitute the five conditions.
Among these five, if the culmination is lacking, it is merely termed an affliction (*kleśa*), as good and evil are diametrically opposed.
The formation of karma is likewise. Regarding the mention of "generosity and precepts," this refers to when one observes the ten wholesome paths of action and extensively practices giving.
Consequently, one is reborn in the heavens of the desire realm, where food and clothing appear spontaneously, palaces follow one’s person, and one is surrounded by a retinue of attendants.
Such karmic fruits arise from generosity. Furthermore, the longevity of devas and humans results from the observance of the precepts. Now, as for the aforementioned "ten wholesome paths," this—

Furthermore, regarding what is called "precepts," these may be either the *upavāsa* (fasting) precepts or the monastic precepts (*pravrajyā-śīla*) and so forth, as explained in the *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness).
It states that one may observe the *upavāsa* precepts for one day and one night, or the *śrāmaṇera* (novice) precepts, the *bhikṣu* (fully ordained monk) precepts, and so on.

Therefore, they are mentioned separately. As for the word "etcetera" (ādi), it includes patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative concentration (dhyāna), or other wholesome dharmas, such as making offerings to the Triple Gem, being filial toward one's parents, and practicing the eight fields of merit. However, the ten wholesome actions alone constitute the direct cause.

The rest are all auxiliary causes. Since this is cultivated with a mind that is still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), one does not escape saṃsāra; it is not like that of a Bodhisattva, who penetrates the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
As for the statement regarding birth in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth: "heaven" is spoken of in a general sense. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

they are named for their radiant purity, sovereignty, and divine efficacy. Taken collectively, they constitute the three realms; taken specifically, they comprise twenty-eight heavens. Namely, the desire...

There are six heavens in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), eighteen heavens in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and four heavens in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding the "realm of desire":

it is so called because of [the craving for] food and drink, sleep, and sexual passion; hence, it is named the realm of desire. As for the "six heavens," the first is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
These are the ministers and attendants of Śakra, who dwell on the four sides of Mount Sumeru, forty-two thousand *yojanas* above the earth.
One *yojana* (one *yojana* equals forty *li*). Their body height is half a *yojana*. Their clothing weighs half a *liang*.
Their lifespan is five hundred years. Fifty human years constitute one day and night. Their yin and yang follow the patterns of the human world.
Second, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (here translated as "Thirty-three"). They dwell upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. This Mount Sumeru rises eighty-four thousand *yojanas* above the waters.
The four lower Heaven Kings dwell halfway up the mountain. Atop the summit, the terrain is level and expansive on all sides;
in each of the four directions there are eight heavens, with one central heaven where Śakra resides. Thus, they are collectively called the Trāyastriṃśa (Thirty-three) Heavens.
The inhabitants of this heaven are one yojana in height, their garments weigh six *zhū*, and their lifespan is one thousand years. By human reckoning...

One hundred human years constitute one day and night. They take mutual embracing as their manifestation of yin and yang. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three) is here called the "Time-Division" (Kāmadhātu).
Because they take the opening and closing of lotus flowers as their day and night, it is called the "Time-Division. It is situated above the preceding heaven, being twice its size;
the inhabitants are two *yojanas* tall, their garments weigh three *zhu*, and their lifespan is two thousand years. By human reckoning, this is twenty... [years].
One human year constitutes one day and night. They engage in union by merely holding each other close. There are four Tuṣita heavens;

this is translated as "Contentment," for they are always content with the pleasures they receive. Their dwellings are twice the size of the previous [heaven], their bodies are four yojanas tall, and their lifespan is four thousand years.
Four hundred human years constitute one day and night. They engage in union by holding hands.

Fifth is the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*). Because they emanate their own objects of enjoyment according to their mental inclinations and then enjoy them themselves, it is called "Delighting in Emanations.

It is situated twice as high as Tuṣita. Their bodies are eight *yojanas* in height; their garments weigh one *zhu*. Their lifespan is eight thousand years. Eight hundred human years constitute one day and night.
They distinguish the seasons by looking at each other’s facial expressions. Sixth is the Heaven of Mastery over Others’ Emanations (*Paranirmitavaśavartin*).
This refers to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin [Heaven], so called because they enjoy the objects of pleasure created by others. They dwell at twice the height of the previous heaven;
their bodies are sixteen yojanas tall, and their garments weigh half a *zhu*. Their lifespan is sixteen thousand years, with one thousand six hundred human years constituting a single day and night.
A mere blink of an eye constitutes a cycle of *yin* and *yang*. From this point downward, it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Thus it is said.
Regarding "practicing the four dhyānas and eight samādhis": *dhyāna* in Sanskrit is translated here as *zhènglǜ* (静虑, "meditative concentration"). The *Fayuan zhang* states:

"As for 'quiet' (*jing*), it means the nature is free from the dust of clamor and obstacles such as sinking and agitation; as for 'concentration' (*lü*), it means focusing the mind with single-minded intent to deliberate upon the gateway of objects."
However, the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti) possess tranquility (śamatha) but lack investigation (vicāra), because they consist solely of a concentrated mind.

The meditative concentration (samādhi) of the desire realm possesses investigation but lacks tranquility, because it is largely characterized by distraction. Only within the form realm are tranquility and investigation balanced; therefore, it receives this name. Regarding the "four dhyānas":

the first is the dhyāna with directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra). Directed thought and sustained thought are also termed initial application (vitakka) and sustained application (vicāra). They serve as the antidote to the desire realm.

Because it is the realm of unwholesome and non-virtuous dharmas. However, *vitarka* (applied thought) is defined by its coarse aspect, while *vicāra* (sustained thought) is defined by its subtle aspect.

Second is the dhyāna without *vitarka* and without *vicāra*, which is so called because it arises from joy (*prīti*) while being free from the mental states of *vitarka* and *vicāra* belonging to the preceding first dhyāna.

Third is the dhyāna free from joy, which is so called because it is free from the joyful mind of the preceding two dhyānas; having abandoned both sorrow and joy, one dwells in the feeling of bliss (*sukha-vedanā*). Fourth is the freedom from joy...
The joy of dhyāna is distinct from the joy and bliss of the first three dhyānas, because both pleasure and pain have been forgotten.

Regarding the "eight attainments," following the four dhyānas, the four formless (ārūpya) empty-attainments are added. These are: first, the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Having now transcended all perceptions of form that existed within the previous realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Second, the [attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness]...

In the meditative attainments of the formless spheres (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the preceding stages of infinite space and the form realm are both not separate from consciousness; now, having transcended them all, one dwells solely in infinite consciousness.
In the third attainment, that of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there was previously a consciousness in which one could dwell; now, even that consciousness cannot be apprehended.
Because both mind and objects are entirely non-existent, the fourth absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is so called;
for while the preceding states were able to eliminate the perception of mind and consciousness, here that too is absent.

This is designated as "absorption" (samādhi) together with the four dhyānas because within the four dhyānas there is a partial definition of absorption, and thus they receive the name "absorption. As for the statement regarding birth in the form and formless realms, it is due to...
By practicing the four dhyānas, one attains birth in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). It is called the "Form Realm" because it possesses the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of a physical body.
Regarding its eighteen heavens: these refer to the three heavens of the First Dhyāna. First is the Brahmakāyika Heaven, which consists of the subjects of the Brahmā King.
Second is the Brahmapurohita Heaven, which consists of the ministers and assistants of the Brahmā King. Third is the Mahābrahmā Heaven, which is the Brahmā King himself. Thus, these three heavens—

All have a lifespan of one kalpa. From this point upward, their bodies and clothing appear according to their wishes; there are no longer distinctions between male and female, and they take the joy of dhyāna and the Dharma as their food.
Because they possess internal mental activity consisting of vitarka and vicāra, they are externally destroyed by the calamity of fire. This refers to the Second Dhyāna.
The three heavens of Limited Light, Immeasurable Light, and Radiant Sound have a lifespan of two kalpas; because they possess internal joy, they are destroyed by external calamities of water.
The three heavens of the Third Dhyāna—Limited Purity, Immeasurable Purity, and Universal Purity—have a lifespan known as three kalpas.

Because they possess internal bliss, the fourth dhyāna is destroyed by the calamity of wind. It consists of nine heavens: the Cloudless (Anabhraka), the Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava), and the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) heavens—these three have a lifespan of four kalpas;

the Heaven of Non-Perception (Asaṃjñisattva) has a lifespan of five hundred kalpas; the Without-Affliction (Avṛha) heaven has a lifespan of one thousand kalpas; the Without-Heat (Atapa) heaven has a lifespan of two thousand kalpas;

the Good Appearance (Sudṛśa) heaven has a lifespan of three thousand kalpas; the Good Vision (Sudarśana) heaven has a lifespan of four thousand kalpas; and the Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha) heaven has a lifespan of five [thousand kalpas].
For a thousand kalpas, one cultivates the latter four dhyānas and is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Formless" means that there is no coarse aggregate of form;
rather, one dwells in the four aggregates of mind and mental factors, supported by meditative concentration. This is called the formless realm. Its four heavens are:

first, the Heaven of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), with a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas; second, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), with a lifespan of twenty... [thousand kalpas].

Ten thousand kalpas. The gods of the Third Sphere of Nothingness have a lifespan of forty-two thousand kalpas. The Fourth Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception has a lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas.

(The various realms of the three miserable paths and the heavens of humans differ in their categories; the realms of desire, form, and formlessness differ according to their respective levels. As for the note stating that [Confucius and Laozi] did not reach [these matters] through sight or hearing: this is because the paradises, hells, and the realm of ghosts were not discussed by Confucius and Laozi, as they were not seen by the eyes of the common world. Heaven.

The fundamental is the [sentient] self; humans and animals are the derivative. People of the world merely know that humans, animals, plants, and trees are produced by Heaven; they do not know that humans and animals are summoned by their own karma, yet they falsely claim they are born of Heaven. This is to be ignorant of the derivative, let alone being able to know what the fruits of that Heaven and so forth truly are.

Even if one were to speak of them, it would not go beyond saying that pure qi ascends, becoming lofty, brilliant, and enduring, characterized by being without sound or smell as the ultimate state. Furthermore, they do not believe in the Buddha’s teachings which can exhaustively reveal the reality of heaven and earth.
Therefore, it is said: how could they be willing to investigate the fundamental? How much less could they know that the empty arises from Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble in the ocean?

Therefore, it is called the Teaching for Humans and Devas (*manuṣya-deva-śāsana*). (Now, karma is of three kinds: first, evil; second, wholesome; and third, immovable. Retribution occurs at three times: retribution in the present life, retribution in the next life, and retribution in subsequent lives.)

(Note: This distinguishes the differences in karmic retribution. "Karma" (*karman*) has the meaning of "constructive activity. However, its essence is both provisional and real. Physical and vocal actions are provisional; volition (*cetanā*) is the real essence. Yet, there are three types of volition: deliberation (*santīraṇa*), determination (*niścaya*), and incitement (*abhyutsāha*).

Only when one actually takes up incitement does it constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*). That is to say, the volition that moves the body is the reality of bodily karma; the volition that issues speech is the reality of vocal karma. The two types of volition—deliberation and determination—are merely the preliminary means. Note on "one evil": this refers to the ten unwholesome paths of action of the first three grades.)

The second, wholesome karma (*kuśala-karman*), refers to the aforementioned five precepts, the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*), and so forth. The third, immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*), refers to the aforementioned four dhyānas and eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); they receive the name "immovable" because, in contrast to the agitation of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are unshakable.

Regarding the statement that retribution (*vipāka*) also has three periods and so forth: retribution is defined by the sense of recompensing a cause. First, immediate retribution (*drstadharma-vipāka*): when one performs evil or good deeds in the present life and receives the retribution in the present body—such as taking a potent medicine for a wolf or tiger that shows its effect immediately.

This applies to actions performed with an extremely intense and sharp mind, whereby immediate retribution is obtained. For example, King Virūḍhaka (Vairūḍyaka) exterminated the Śākya clan and fell alive into the Avīci Hell; likewise, the Dharma-teacher Fanzhao single-mindedly recited the name of Amitābha and was reborn in Sukhāvatī upon death, without passing through an intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Second, retribution in the next life (*upapadya-vipāka*): performing actions in this life and receiving the retribution in the next life.

Receiving retribution: it is like sowing wheat this year and harvesting it the following year. Regarding "retribution in the third life" (post-natal retribution): this refers to karma created in the present life that is received only after an intervening birth. It is like being in debt to two people; the stronger claimant is paid first. If the wholesome is light and the unwholesome is heavy, one first receives the retribution for the unwholesome;

if the unwholesome is light and the wholesome is heavy, one first receives the retribution for the wholesome. Thus, that which is received later constitutes "post-natal retribution. This is based on the intermingling of good and evil, further distinguished by their relative weight as to whether they occur earlier or later.

Other sutras and treatises state that, in addition to these three, there is "indeterminate retribution," which involves a detailed examination of the timing of its maturation. Furthermore, there are four permutations: (1) determinate in time but indeterminate in retribution; (2) determinate in retribution but indeterminate in time; (3) determinate in both time and retribution; and (4) indeterminate in both time and retribution, and so forth.
According to this teaching, karma is the root of the body;
one merely knows that this body is summoned by karma, yet does not further investigate from where karma itself arises. This is truly due to dull faculties.
I have not yet been able to investigate this thoroughly.
Now I question you: since one receives a body in the five realms of existence by virtue of having created karma, I wonder who it is that creates the karma and who it is that receives the retribution?
"Who creates and who experiences? This is a general inquiry. He should answer: "It is my body and mind that are able to create. Therefore, the following is a specific refutation:
If it were these eyes, ears, hands, and feet that could perform actions, then in a person who has just died, the eyes, ears, hands, and feet would still be perfectly intact.
"Why do you not see or hear [the agent] performing [the action]?

This is a challenge to the body. This objection arises because [the opponent] fails to understand that the body and so forth are merely conventional designations, and instead clings to them as being a real agent;
thus, they raise this challenge.
If it is said that the mind creates [the world], what is this mind?

This is a difficult question regarding the mind. In the Buddha’s teachings, four kinds of mind are explained: first, the physical heart (*māṃsapiṇḍa-citta*), which is the fire within the five viscera;
second, the cognitive mind (*ālambana-citta*), which comprises the eight consciousnesses, as all are capable of cognizing their respective objects; third...
The "accumulating mind" refers exclusively to the *ālaya-vijñāna*, for it accumulates all seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).

The "solid and substantial mind" is precisely the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*. People of the present day and heavens do not understand these latter three [minds], and thus they encounter this difficulty.
This is largely the same as what is commonly referred to in the world as "the mind.
If one speaks of the physical heart, the physical heart has substance and is bound within the body; how could it then swiftly enter the eyes and ears to discern right and wrong in external matters?
If one does not know right from wrong, on what basis could one choose between acceptance and rejection?

Regarding the statement that [the mind] has substance: because the "fleshly ball of mind" (*māṃsapiṇḍa-citta*) belongs to the category of form (*rūpa-dharma*), it is merely the basis for the mind and its associates and lacks any real functional activity.
How, then, could it enter the eyes or ears so swiftly? However, the Buddha taught that the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has two types of functions:
first, it operates simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses; for example, when the eye perceives a form, the mind also perceives that form and performs discrimination.
[One] distinguishes between black and white [right and wrong], giving rise to extraordinary resolve. The cases of the ear perceiving sound and so forth are analogous.

Second, that which does not arise simultaneously with the five consciousnesses is called "independent mental consciousness" (*manas*). For example, when the aforementioned five [consciousnesses] do not perceive objects, there is internal reflection and so forth;

yet people today, within the teachings of humans and devas, do not recognize that the perception of external objects is the function of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), but instead cling to it as being the [substantial] mind itself. Therefore, this [error] is summoned.

This is difficult to explain. Furthermore, since the mind and the eyes, ears, hands, and feet are all characterized by material obstruction (*sapratigha*), how could they possibly communicate internally and externally, coordinate their movements and responses,
and together create karmic conditions?

This demonstrates that the "flesh-ball mind" (māṃsapiṇḍa-citta) has no functional activity. If it were to possess such activity, then the lungs and other organs would likewise do so; consequently, those who have already died should still be able to engage in cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*).

If you argue that it is merely emotions such as joy, anger, love, and hatred that incite the body and speech to perform actions, [then consider] these emotions of joy, anger, and so forth— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical argumentation regarding the non-functionality of the physical heart as a locus of consciousness.*
Arising and ceasing momentarily, it lacks an inherent essence of its own; how could it serve as a master to perform actions?

Those whose minds are deluded often mistake the emotions for the mind, and consequently claim that the mind itself can experience joy and anger, love and hatred, and that it initiates the actions of body and speech, thereby creating karma.
They fail to realize that joy, anger, and so forth are merely mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
How could that which is produced by the mental factors (caitta) be the mind-king (cittarāja)? Furthermore, emotions such as joy and anger arise and cease momentarily;

when encountering objects of a favorable nature, one feels joy and attachment, while when encountering objects of an unfavorable nature, one feels anger and aversion. These arise only when the objects appear.

When objects depart, they cease; yet the essence of the mind is eternal and fundamentally free from arising or ceasing. If the mind were non-existent when objects depart, the mind would be annihilated.
Who then would be the sovereign who performs actions?
He further said: "One should not investigate in this way, thinking that it is my very body and mind that are the agents of action.
This body has already died; who then experiences the retribution of pleasure and pain?"
Previously, the body and mind were analyzed through division; here, they are analyzed through synthesis. Suppose the opponent should offer this defense:
"It is not appropriate to investigate by analyzing them separately in this way. It is my body and my mind, taken together as a whole, that constitute the agent.
Therefore, when the body dies and the mind ceases, who is it that receives retribution? If he were to concede that the mind does not cease, then this objection would not arise.
If one were to say that there is another body after death, how could the body and mind of today create evil or cultivate merit,
causing the body and mind of another future life to experience suffering or joy?

Suppose they offer this defense: "Although the previous body has died, there still remains a subsequent body; since the previous body created the karma and the subsequent body receives the retribution, what fault is there?
The objection states: "If the mind does not perish, then 'one creates and one receives' would apply to a single person."

From the perspective of principle, this may be acceptable; however, since you now maintain that both body and mind perish together, the subsequent body and mind would not be the same as the preceding body and mind.
It would be improper for one to act and another to experience the result. This is like a former official who perverts the law and a subsequent official who is consequently dismissed.
How could such a principle exist?
Based on this, those who cultivate merit are utterly wronged, while those who commit transgressions are exceedingly fortunate. How can the divine principle be so devoid of righteousness?
To cultivate merit in this present life, yet suffer its consequences due to evil committed in a previous existence—is this not a grievance?
To commit evil in this present life, yet enjoy its rewards due to goodness performed in a previous existence—is this not a stroke of luck?

The "spiritual principle" (shenli) refers precisely to the principle of karma (*karmadhātu*). Since karma is created by the mind, it is termed "spiritual. The principle of spirit is supremely impartial;
it certainly does not act with such injustice or arbitrariness. It is simply that your own school has been unable to investigate it deeply and instead discusses it according to mere sentiment;
thus, it appears to be unjust.
Therefore, it is known that although one merely practices this teaching and believes in karmic conditions, one does not yet penetrate the fundamental nature of the body;

this serves to clarify that the previous school’s position remains incomplete. Since one already believes in karmic retribution, this is superior to the preceding Confucian and Lao-Zhuang views which cling only to spontaneity (*ziran*), vital breath (*qi*), and destiny (*ming*).

However, one still does not know that karma is created by the mind, and that mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) are momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and continue through a homogeneous succession (*sabhāga-santati*).
Therefore, it is said that they do not comprehend the fundamental nature of the body. The purport of the preceding and following arguments is that each follows upon the other to refute it.

In this case, the followers of the Human and Heavenly [vehicles] take their stand on karmic retribution to perform the refutation; yet karmic retribution is precisely what the Confucians and Daoists are deluded about. Thus, citing karmic retribution alone is sufficient to refute them.
That they have not yet realized that form and mind arise from conditions and so forth is what they are deluded about in this teaching. Subsequently, [the text continues...]
The Lesser Vehicle is further treated as that which is to be refuted.
