Second, regarding the teachings of the Hīnayāna:

"yāna" (vehicle) has the meaning of transporting or conveying. This refers to relying on the teachings of dependent origination to realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), practicing for one's own benefit, and attaining the fruit of the extinction of the ashes (*bhasma-prahāṇa*).
Because it conveys sentient beings out of the three realms (*tridhātu*), it is called a "vehicle. It does not seek the Great [Vehicle].
As for the fruit [of this path], it is called "small" because it lacks the benefit of others.

It describes the form of the physical body and the mind of discursive thought; from beginningless time, through the power of causes and conditions, they arise and perish moment by moment in an endless succession, like the steady flow of a stream or the flickering of a lamp’s flame.

This first section clarifies the causal conditions for the fundamental tenets of that teaching. "The color of the physical form" distinguishes [the body] from the external four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
"The mind of thought and deliberation" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This form and mind constitute the fruits produced through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

To clarify the characteristics of arising and ceasing, one must first explain the causes of arising and ceasing; because they arise through the power of causes and conditions, the six internal consciousnesses serve as the objects.
Regarding "perfuming": the three poisons act as the perfumers. The arising of delusions and the creation of karma serve as the causal conditions for their manifestation.
Since this body and mind are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are subject to the four marks of change and flow. Each preceding moment ceases and each succeeding moment arises;

because the subsequent moments follow upon the preceding ones without interruption, it is like a stream of water that flows continuously. Although it appears as a single current, it does not remain static.
They are severed; yet the preceding flow is not the subsequent flow. It is like a lamp burning its wick: although the single flame does not cease, the preceding flame is not the subsequent flame.

The characteristics of the arising and ceasing of body and mind are likewise so: though the preceding and succeeding moments differ, they do not hinder their continuity from beginningless time until now.
To say "beginningless" is to distinguish this from the non-Buddhist schools that maintain there is a first beginning.
Therefore, because one knows only the present life, the body and mind appear to be a single, permanent entity through their provisional conjunction.
This clarifies that the body and mind are established by relying upon one another. As for "provisional conjunction," it means they depend upon and support each other, like a bundle of reeds.

This means that body and mind constitute two [entities], yet they are not separate from one another; therefore, they are said to be "as if one. They arise and perish in succession, yet they are constantly continuous;
therefore, they are said to be "as if permanent."
Ordinary, ignorant people do not realize this; they grasp at it as a self. Because they treasure this self, they immediately give rise to the three poisons:

greed (such as craving fame and profit to glorify the self), hatred (hatred toward circumstances that oppose one, fearing they will harm the self), and delusion (irrational calculation and deliberation).
Ordinary, ignorant beings do not realize this because they are shrouded by ignorance; thus, they grasp at it as a self, which is the innate grasping for a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).

Cherishing this self is the conceptual grasping for a self (*vikalpa-ātma-grāha*). Based on this grasping, delusions arise; due to this grasping for a self, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) is produced.
The Chapter on the Obstructions of Affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Although these are many, they are summarized as the three poisons because they are predominant.
Greed has the nature of attachment; hatred has the nature of malice and resentment; delusion has the nature of confusion and darkness.

They are called "poisons" by way of metaphor, just as a venomous snake or poisonous medicine inevitably injures one upon contact and surely causes death if ingested. These three are likewise capable of harming sentient beings.
It gives rise to the wisdom-life of the Dharmakāya; therefore, it is called "poison.
The three poisons strike the mind, inciting body and speech to create all karma.
This refers to the arising of karma due to delusion. "Striking" (kī) means to permeate and stir; thus, the three poisons serve as the perfuming agents.
The mental consciousness acts as the perfuming agent, just as wind strikes still water to produce waves.
That which incites the body and speech to perform all karmic actions refers specifically to the ten unwholesome paths of action and so forth.

Since karma once formed cannot be escaped, one accordingly undergoes bodies of suffering and pleasure within the five destinies (induced by individual karma), and occupies superior or inferior locations within the three realms (induced by collective karma).

This refers to the retribution experienced due to causes and karma. There are two types of retribution: the body within the five destinies (*pañcagati*) constitutes the primary retribution (*vipāka*), while the three realms (*tridhātu*) and nine stages (*navabhūmi*) constitute the secondary retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*).
By committing the ten non-virtuous actions, one undergoes the sufferings of the three miserable paths; by practicing the goodness of ethical discipline, one enjoys the pleasures of humans and devas.
Regarding the superiority and inferiority within the three realms: for instance, when comparing the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the form realm is [superior].

Superiority and inferiority: the desire realm is inferior. When comparing the Four Heavenly Kings to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is superior and the Four Heavenly Kings are inferior.

(The note states: those produced by individual karma (*pratyeka-karma*) are so because each person creates and experiences them differently; those produced by collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*) are so because many people create and experience them together.)
Regarding the body one has received, one again clings to it as "self" and again gives rise to craving and so forth, thereby creating karma and undergoing retribution.

This clarifies that the three paths [of affliction, action, and suffering] are uninterrupted. The *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra* Preface states: "Delusions and karmas follow upon one another; retributions and responses revolve in cycles.

Through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, none can stop or sever them. Therefore, the sūtras and śāstras call a person a 'pudgala' (a person who repeatedly takes up existence), meaning..."
Because one repeatedly gives rise to afflictions, creates karma, and undergoes retribution, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the chapter on "Defilement and the Defiled," states:
"The Sūtras say that greed, hatred, and delusion are the roots of the world. It continues: "By means of the three poisons as causes and conditions, the three types of karma arise;
by means of the three types of karma as causes and conditions, the three realms arise. Therefore, all phenomena exist. This may be taken as proof.

Know that the body undergoes birth, old age, sickness, and death; having died, it is born again. The realms (dhātus) undergo formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; having become empty, they form again.

(Regarding how the world is formed at the beginning of the kalpa of emptiness, the verse says: "In the realm of emptiness, a great wind arises; its lateral breadth is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen lakṣas. Nothing, not even a diamond, can destroy it. This is called the 'Wind that Sustains the Realm. The clouds of the Light-Sound Golden Treasury spread forth..."

In the trichiliocosm, rain falls like chariot axles, but the winds obstruct it so that it does not flow away; it is eleven *lakṣa* deep, whereupon the Vajradhātu first forms. Successively, clouds of golden storehouse pour down rain that fills its interior. First, the realm of Brahmā is formed, extending down to the Yāma Heaven.

The winds churn the clear water to form Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, and so forth; the dregs and impurities become the mountain ranges and the earth. The four continents, the hells, the salt ocean, and the outer Cakravāḍa mountains are then established—this is what is called the formation of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). Time passes for one cycle of increase and decrease, until the merit of the second dhyāna is exhausted.

Descending to be born among humans, they initially consumed earth-cakes and forest creepers; later, they could no longer digest non-glutinous rice, and the functions of excrement and urine appeared. Male and female forms became distinct, fields were divided, and lords were established, who then sought ministers and assistants. Through these various distinctions, nineteen cycles of increase and decrease passed;

together with the preceding [period], these constitute twenty total cycles of increase and decrease, which is termed a *vivartakalpa* (the kalpa of formation). The commentary states: Within the kalpa of the empty realm (*ākāśadhātu*), this refers to the Daoist teaching known as the Way of Non-being (*xuwu*). However, the essence of the Dao is quiescent illumination and spiritual penetration; it is not non-being. Perhaps Laozi was confused by this, or perhaps he established it as a provisional device.

One must strive to sever human desires; therefore, the realm of emptiness (*ākāśa*) is pointed to as the Way (*mārga*). Within the realm of emptiness there is a great wind, which is precisely that primordial undifferentiated breath (*hun-tun*); thus it is said that "the Way gives birth to the One. That which is called the "Golden Treasury" is the beginning of spirit and form, which is the Great Ultimate (*taiji*).

When rain falls but does not flow, it is because the Yin energy has congealed; only when Yin and Yang unite can generation and completion occur. The realm of Brahmā and Mount Sumeru are his heavens. The turbid dregs are the earth; this is the "One giving birth to the Two. When the merit of the Second Dhyāna heaven is exhausted and one is reborn below, this is humanity;

this is the "Two giving birth to the Three," and thus the Three Powers (*sancái*) are complete. From the "earth-cakes" and so forth down to the various [stages of evolution], this is the "Three giving birth to the myriad things. This corresponds to the period prior to the Three August Ones (*sanhhuang*), a time when people lived in caves and dwelt in the wilds, and the transformation by fire had not yet occurred. It was simply because of that time.

There is no written record [of this]. Consequently, later generations have transmitted it with unclear details, leading to successive errors and various divergent theories among the works of different schools. Furthermore, Buddhism generally elucidates the three thousandfold world system and is not restricted to the Great Tang; thus, its internal and external doctrines do not entirely coincide with those of other traditions.

As for "abiding" (sthāna), it refers to the kalpa of abiding (*sthiti-kalpa*), which likewise consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease. As for "destruction" (saṃvarta), it refers to the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), which also consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease: the first nineteen cycles of increase and decrease destroy sentient beings, while the final cycle of increase and decrease destroys the physical world (*bhājana-loka*). The agents of destruction are the three calamities of water, fire, and wind.

As for "emptiness" (śūnya), it refers to the kalpa of emptiness (*śūnya-kalpa*), which likewise consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease; during this interval, there is no world or sentient beings.

This specifically elucidates the characteristics of the fruit [of conditioned existence]. The initial arising of the five aggregates is called birth (*jāti*). The maturation, decay, and transformation of the aggregates is called aging (*jarā*).

The increase and decrease of the four great elements constitutes illness (*vyādhi*). The disintegration and destruction of the five aggregates is called death (*maraṇa*). These four characteristics of the body are produced by individual karma.

The completion of a fruit through the convergence of various conditions is called formation (*saṃbhava*). Its temporary reliance upon support is called subsistence (*sthiti*). Its destruction through the three calamities is called dissolution (*bhaṅga*).
To be vast and devoid of any thing is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). The world possesses four phases, which are induced by collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*).

Birth and death continue in succession, with the phases of formation and destruction following one another in an endless cycle; such is the natural law (*dharmatā*). (Note: A separate explanation of the states of the world’s formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness follows.

First, the period of formation is described at length, citing a verse from the *Abhidharmakośa*: "As for the realm of emptiness, it is the twentieth kalpa of emptiness following the kalpa of destruction of the preceding world-system. Furthermore, this realm of emptiness is the 'wheel of emptiness' (*ākāśa-maṇḍala*). In Sanskrit it is *koṭi*, which here means 'hundred million' [or 'extreme limit']. This refers to...)

The wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala) is sixteen hundred million [yojanas] in thickness. The Abhidharma-śāstra states: "Twenty kalpas after the world has been empty, when it is about to be formed, the Vairambha winds blow and form the wind-circle.

It is situated at the very bottom with a thickness of nine hundred and sixty thousand yojanas, and a breadth of twelve hundred and thirty-four thousand five hundred yojanas. Although there are slight differences in these measurements, they are generally the same in that the wind-circle resides at the bottom. Because its power is so great, even diamond cannot destroy it.

The Golden Treasury (*Suvarṇagarbha*). It is called "Golden" because its color is like gold and it pours forth water inexhaustibly; hence it is termed the "Golden Treasury. When clouds ascend as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they rain down in torrents like axles, which accumulate upon that wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) and coalesce into the water-circle (*jala-maṇḍala*).

The uppermost part of this water-circle solidifies into gold, like the film that forms on the surface of milk when it stands still; this constitutes the Gold Wheel (*kāñcana-cakra*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states that the thickness of the water-circle is eight *lakṣas*.

Furthermore, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states that the mass of water is six hundred thousand *yojanas* thick. Above the water, a great wind blows and churns this water, forming gold on its surface like the cream that rises from boiled milk; this is called the Gold Wheel. Its thickness is three *lakṣas* and twenty thousand *yojanas*. Regarding the citation of eleven *lakṣas* in the treatise, this includes the entire eight [lakṣas] of the water-circle.

The *loka* [world-system] and the three *loka*s of the Golden Wheel (*kāñcana-cakra*) thus constitute eleven. This meaning clarifies that the Golden Wheel rests upon the Water Wheel; the Water Wheel rests upon the Wind Wheel; and the Wind Wheel rests upon the Space Wheel. The Space Wheel is at the very bottom, and the Golden Wheel is at the very top.

Once these three wheels are formed, rain falls from the sky onto the Golden Wheel, flowing incessantly day and night like a river pouring forth. For countless thousands of years, the water becomes two hundred and forty thousand *yojana*s thick, twelve billion three hundred and forty-five thousand *yojana*s wide, and thirty-six billion one thousand three hundred and fifty *yojana*s in circumference.
The wind blows this water, causing the pure essence to rise upward. From the top down to the bottom, it forms in succession the Brahmā Heaven of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, the four heavens of the sky-dwellers in the desire realm are formed; next, Mount Sumeru and the seven golden mountains are established, with the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven residing at the summit of Sumeru and the Cāturmahārājika Heaven residing halfway up Sumeru.

As for the seven golden mountains: first, Yugandhara; second, Īṣādhara; third, Khadiraka; fourth, Sudarśana; fifth, Aśvakarṇa; sixth, Vinataka; and seventh, Nimindhara. Since these seven mountains are all composed of gold, they are called the "seven golds.

Sumeru stands in the center, surrounded by the seven gold mountains; this region lies between the clear and the turbid. That which belongs to the most turbid, thick mud-like elements coagulates to form the Great Earth, the various mountains, and the level plains.

There are then the four continents, as well as the hells, the salt ocean, and the outer rim; only then is the receptacle world established. The four continents are: first, Pūrvavideha (Eastern Victory Body); second, Jambudvīpa (Southern Rose-Apple Continent); third, Aparagoyānī (Western Cow-Grass Continent); and fourth, Uttarakuru (Northern Kurus).

These four dwell within the salt ocean at the four sides of Mount Sumeru; they are what are called "islands" (*tiṅzhǔ*). Hence, they are termed the "Four Continents. *Niraya* is the name for the hells. The "Salt Ocean" is the sea upon which the Four Continents rely;

its water is salty, unlike the fragrant seas (*xiānghǎi*) situated between the seven golden mountains. The "Outer Rim" refers to the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), which lie further outside the Salt Ocean; all are composed of turbid sediment. The above provides a general explanation of the characteristics of the formation of the physical world (*bhājanaloka*).

A single Great Transformation Buddha rules over one trichiliocosm; these are established simultaneously. When it is said that "a period of one increase and decrease has passed," this refers to the time when the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand years and decreased by one year every hundred years until it reached ten years;

this is called the *kṣaya-kalpa* (the aeon of decrease). Then, from a lifespan of ten years, it increases by one year every hundred years until it reaches eighty-four thousand years; this is called the *vivarta-kalpa* (the aeon of increase). It takes such a length of time for the physical world (*bhājana-loka*) to be established. At this time, the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, having exhausted their celestial merit, fall into the human realm and are born there.

Their bodies possess radiance, they travel freely through the air, they take joy as their sustenance, and they possess mind-made bodies produced by transformation. At this time, the great oceans rise and fall, opening up paths through rivers and plains where the waters had previously stood.

As the earth-sustenance diminished, the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) emerged, possessing the fragrance, color, and exquisite taste of fine honey. Furthermore, the "earth-crust" (*pṛthivī-maṇḍa*), also called the "earth-cake," arose; once the earth-flavor was exhausted, forest creepers (*vanalatā*) grew, which all people consumed.

Because of their greed for food, they consequently lost their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and their radiance also diminished. The world became dark. Out of compassion, the Bodhisattvas manifested the sun, moon, and stars to provide illumination. The *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* states: the Bodhisattva Ratnamati became the Sun Deity (*Sūryadevaputra*);

the Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī became the Moon Deity (*Candradevaputra*); and the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabha became the Star Palace Deity (*Tārakāmandaladevaputra*). When the forest creepers vanished, non-glutinous rice (*śāli*) grew, sprouting again in the evening after being harvested in the morning. Due to eating this grain, excrement and urine appeared, male and female forms were differentiated, and sensual desire flourished.

Human civilization was thus established. People vied with one another to harvest rice, storing it for their own sustenance; consequently, the strong oppressed the weak, and there was no one to restrain them. They gathered together to deliberate and appointed a wise man as the lord of the land and fields, providing him with common contributions.

As the lord could not govern alone, he sought ministers and assistants, leading to the emergence of various distinctions, such as palaces, cities, walls, boats, carriages, clothing, and utensils. After nineteen cycles of increase and decrease, human principles were finally perfected. These twenty cycles of increase and decrease preceding the completion are collectively termed a *vivartakalpa* (the kalpa of formation).

Once formed, it remains stable (*sthāyikalpa*); once stable, it decays (*saṃvartakalpa*); and once decayed, it becomes empty (*śūnyakalpa*). Each of these periods likewise consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease. Altogether, these eighty cycles of increase and decrease constitute one great *mahākalpa*. Within the period of decay, during the first nineteen cycles of increase and decrease, the process of destruction occurs.

Regarding the subsequent increase and decrease that destroys the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) and the sentient beings (*sattva-loka*): at the end of one *antarakalpa* of decrease, when the human lifespan is thirty years, the calamity of famine arises. It lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days.

Due to the rising of violent winds that blow upon those regions, the seasons lose their regularity and the five grains fail to grow; thus, famine ensues. When the human lifespan is twenty years, the calamity of pestilence arises. Due to malevolent spirits and demons who inflict harm upon people, it lasts for seven months and seven days before ceasing.

When the human lifespan is ten years, the calamity of weapons arises. All grasses and trees are transformed into blades and weapons, and they slaughter one another; they use only these weapons as their own adornments. It lasts for seven days and seven nights before ceasing. At that time, there would be no sentient beings remaining in the world.

Regarding the destruction of the receptacle world: first, when the fire calamity arises, it destroys up to the First Dhyāna. When seven suns appear in the sky, the great earth and Mount Sumeru both emit flames and burn completely at once. Due to that heat, they draw up the water wheel from below.

The waters are like clarified butter (*sarpis*); all are exhausted. After seven cycles of calamities by fire, a calamity by water arises, destroying up to the Second Dhyāna Heaven. The sixteenth moment of mind—the eighth path of liberation—is termed the "fruit of stream-entry" (*srotāpatti-phala*). In this state, there are two aspects of mental activity: first, abiding correctly in the fruit; [second,] not yet having abandoned [the remaining afflictions].

The afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) all belong to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). The two subsequent fruits of cultivation belong to the path of meditation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Having abandoned six grades of the afflictions of the desire realm through six uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) and five paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one is termed a candidate for the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*).

The sixth path of liberation is termed the fruit of once-returner (because one returns to the desire realm only once). Having abandoned the final three grades [of afflictions] through three uninterrupted paths and two paths of liberation, one is termed a candidate for the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*).
The third liberation is called the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), because one will no longer return to take birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Having abandoned the seventy-two categories of afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the two higher realms—there being eight stages in those two realms with nine categories in each stage—one attains seventy-two paths of uninterrupted realization (*ānantaryamārga*) and seventy-one paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*);

this is called the stage of the candidate for arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*). (All preceding stages belong to the path of cultivation, *bhāvanāmārga*). The seventy-second path of liberation is called...
The fruit of arhatship. One who realizes the fivefold Dharma-body is designated as being in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). In the Sanskrit language, it is *arhat* or *arahat*;

this is translated here as "one who is worthy" (*yogya*). There are three meanings of "worthy": first, one is worthy because one has already eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, because one should not undergo further existence in a physical body; third, because one should receive the sublime offerings of devas and humans.

Regarding the phrase "extinguishing the body and extinguishing wisdom," Master Zhao said: "No affliction is greater than having a body; therefore, one extinguishes the body to return to non-existence.
No toil is greater than having wisdom; therefore, one cuts off wisdom to dissolve into the void. Wisdom is an affliction for the body, and the body...

Exhausted by the toil of wisdom, they wander the long path of saṃsāra without ceasing their weariness. Therefore, once those of the Hīnayāna have attained the four fruits, they employ the fire of transformation to cremate their bodies;
body and wisdom both perish, and they enter the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*) to experience the bliss of cessation (*nirvāṇa*).
According to the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha should be listed here. In Sanskrit, they are called *Pratyekabuddha*; in this [language], it means...

The Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer), also called the Pratyayabuddha (Conditionally Awakened). As for the "Solitary Realizer": appearing in a world where no Buddha exists, they observe the dharma of causes and conditions and attain awakening through their own power without a teacher;

thus they are named "Solitary Realizers. If, however, they hear the dharma of causes and conditions from a Buddha and perform the contemplation of the seventy-seven knowledges regarding the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), they are called "Conditionally Awakened.
They sever the delusions of the three realms and partially subdue the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) by means of their faculties.

Because of their keen faculties, they surpass the Arhats and attain the fifth fruit. They incinerate their bodies with transformed fire and enter the realm of the unconditioned; thus they are called Pratyekabuddhas.

As for why the treatise does not explain them separately: it is because they are identical to the aforementioned Śrāvakas in their contemplation of the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), in their severance of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and in their realization of the fruit of "ashes and severance" (*kṣaya-phala*). Therefore, they are not mentioned separately.
Within this school, it is held that the two dharmas of form and mind, along with greed, hatred, and delusion, constitute the root of the body, the environment, and the world.
This concludes the summary of the Hīnayāna school. The *Dàochǎo* states: "The Hīnayāna calculates the root of birth and death; although there are many [factors]..."

Regarding the meaning, three points are briefly set forth. First, the reckoning of matter and mind: as stated in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, the Sautrāntika masters reckon present matter, mind, and other dharmas as the causes of defilement and purification.
This implies that, just as in the Mahāyāna, the eighth consciousness serves as the "perfumable" (*bhāvyamāna*).
Second, the three poisons as cause: the meaning is that they function as "perfumers" (*bhāvaka*) as in the Mahāyāna. The Āgama says: "Greed, hatred..."
Ignorance is the root of this world, and so forth. These three points combine the meanings of the two preceding [sections]:

they agree with the Mahāyāna in that there must be both the perfumed (*bhāvya*) and the perfumer (*bhāvaka*) for the process of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) to occur. If this is so, how does it differ from the Mahāyāna?

Because [in your system] only the six consciousnesses serve as the perfumed, and not the eighth; even if you speak of the *ālayavijñāna*, it exists only in name. Furthermore, the perfumers are not the seven [consciousnesses].
Consciousness is therefore entirely different [from the other aggregates].
Regarding the past and future, there is no separate dharma that serves as their basis.
This uses the present to illustrate the other two time periods; they all equally take matter, mind, and the three poisons as their basis, with nothing else.

Regarding this Dharma, I now challenge [the opponent] as follows: As for that which serves as the fundamental basis for the self throughout successive lifetimes, its own essence must be uninterrupted.
This is refuted by the meaning of the Mahāyāna. To say that its own essence must be uninterrupted is as explained in the Mahāyāna.
Because it is the eighth consciousness, the *Treatise* states: "It perpetually evolves like a torrential stream. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The element from time beginningless, the support for all phenomena. Since it says "from time beginningless," one knows that it is uninterrupted.

Now, the five consciousnesses do not arise when their conditions are lacking (the sense organs, objects, etc., acting as conditions). The mental consciousness does not sometimes function (during fainting, sleep, the attainment of cessation, the attainment of non-conception, or in the realm of non-conceptual beings).
Regarding the statement that the five consciousnesses do not arise when their conditions are deficient: according to the Mahāyāna teaching, visual consciousness arises from nine conditions:

first, space; second, light; third, the sense organ; fourth, the object; fifth, attention (*manasikāra*); sixth, discrimination; seventh, defilement or purity; eighth, the fundamental [consciousness]; and ninth, the seeds.

Auditory consciousness arises from eight conditions, which are the same as the aforementioned nine with the exception of light. The three consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body each arise from seven conditions.

This means that among the aforementioned eight [consciousnesses], "space" (*ākāśa*) is excluded. (Note: The "medium faculty" (*madhyendriya*) refers to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); the "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). These two are mentioned briefly because they represent the other conditions; if even one of these conditions is lacking, consciousness cannot arise.

Regarding what is called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*), it refers to the "independent mental consciousness" (*svatantra-manovijñāna*). (Note: Five states in which it does not function are cited: the two states of fainting and deep sleep—these are spoken of in relation to the lower realms—and the two meditative attainments of the non-conceptual and the cessation—these are spoken of in relation to the higher realms.

Specifically, in the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), mental and sensory perceptions do not arise; this is the meditative state sought by non-Buddhists. As for the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it is called "cessation" because the preceding six and seventh consciousnesses do not arise at all.)

This meditative absorption is attained only by noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding the sequence of the two absorptions, one should first attain the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*). What is called the "heaven of non-conception" (*asaṃjñisattva*) refers precisely to the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-conception; that is to say, within this heaven, it is a place where the sixth consciousness, along with its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*), does not function.
Regarding these five stages, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not function in them.
As for the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they lack these four great elements (*mahābhūta*); how then can they maintain this body so that it remains unbroken from lifetime to lifetime?

The four heavens of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are entirely devoid of coarse matter (*rūpa*). Because they possess only the four aggregates (*skandha*)—namely, the mind and its mental factors—they receive the name "formless.
Since the preceding five consciousnesses and the sixth consciousness do not arise or function there, it is "without mind" (*acitta*); this is precisely what is meant by "formless.
They [the opponents] reckon that matter and mind are fundamental; now that both are absent, by what means would this body be maintained without interruption?
In the Mahāyāna, since the existence of an eighth consciousness is accepted, the problem regarding the meaning of "sustaining the seeds" does not arise.
Thus, we know that even those who specialize in this teaching have not yet fundamentally examined the nature of the person (the *pudgala*).
This teaching of the Hīnayāna is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
As for the Mahāyāna teachings on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),

they consist in fully cultivating the two benefits (*dvaya-hita*) and fully realizing the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), carrying one across to enlightenment (*bodhi*) and nirvāṇa, reaching their ultimate consummation.

The "Shore" (Kāṇḍa). To distinguish it from the preceding "Small" [Vehicle], it is called the Mahāyāna. It provides an extensive exposition of all phenomena, hence it is named the Teaching on the Characteristics of Phenomena (Dharmalakṣaṇa-śāsana).
It teaches that all sentient beings have, from time immemorial, naturally possessed eight kinds of consciousness.
This first provides a general indication of the fundamental tenets of the Dharma-characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa). The term "all" refers to the five natures (pañcagotra).

The phrase "beginningless, naturally so" distinguishes this from the eighty thousand kalpas and other such views held by non-Buddhists (tīrthika). As for the "eight kinds of consciousness," the first is visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
2. Ear-consciousness; 3. Nose-consciousness; 4. Tongue-consciousness; 5. Body-consciousness; 6. Mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); 7. Manas-consciousness (*manas*;

here translated as "mind," which constantly and critically deliberates, being superior to the other consciousnesses); 8. Ālaya-consciousness (*ālaya*; here translated as "storehouse," so called because it possesses the three meanings of that which stores, that in which things are stored, and that which is clung to as a self).

Among these, the eighth, the ālayavijñāna, is their fundamental basis. It suddenly transforms into the sense organs, the body, the receptacle world, and the seeds, giving rise to the seven consciousnesses;
all of these are able to manifest their own respective objects, yet none possess any real dharmas whatsoever.
Next, the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) are explained in detail regarding their root and branches.

As for the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*, it is called the "root" because this consciousness maintains the seeds of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and linguistic designations (*nāma-pada*); because it serves as the support (*āśraya*) for the seven transforming consciousnesses and their objects;
and because it continues uninterruptedly from cause to fruit. It is specifically named "mind" (*citta*). In Sanskrit, it is *citta*, which means "accumulation."

"Arising" (*utpāda*) is its meaning, because it gives rise to the manifestation of all seeds. It takes as its objects three categories: seeds, the root-body (*mūla-ātmabhāva*), and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). In total, there are three states:
first, the state of being stored through the grasping of self-love (*ātma-sneha*), the name and meaning of which are as previously explained;

second, the state of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma, called *vipāka* in Sanskrit, which here means "ripening. It is so named for three reasons, whereby it is termed "ripening": [text continues].

Maturity [of karma] is threefold: first, maturity at different times, such as when karma created in the past receives its retribution in the present life, or when karma created in the present life receives its retribution in a future life;
second, maturity through transformation, because the cause ceases while the fruit arises; third, maturity through dissimilar types.

Because its causes encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, while its fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is termed *ādhāna*—the Sanskrit for which is translated here as "sustaining" (*zhíchí*).

This refers to its state of continuous sustaining from the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) up until the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), as it sustains both the ordinary and the noble.

Although it transforms into the Perfect Mirror Wisdom within the state of fruition, this is merely a transformation of name and not of substance. Because it possesses these many meanings, [it is so designated].
"It can serve as the basis" means that it functions as the foundation. To say "it suddenly transforms the sense-faculties and the body, etc. explains the meaning of its functioning as the basis.

That which transforms is the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*); that which is transformed consists of the two portions: the seeing-portion (*darśanabhāga*) and the object-portion (*nimittabhāga*). Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Transformation refers to the substance of consciousness revolving and appearing as the two portions, the object and the seeing; both arise based upon the self-verifying portion. Based on these two portions, the notion of 'self' is provisionally established."
Regarding the Dharma: those two [subject and object] are absent therein because there is nothing upon which they could depend.

Furthermore, it is said that "consciousness-only has no objective realm," because objects do not exist and are but false perceptions—just as when a person’s eyes are afflicted by cataracts, they perceive such things as hairs or a second moon.

As for the statement that "the seven consciousnesses arise through transformation," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* quotes the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*: "It is like the vast waves of the ocean, which are stirred up by a violent wind; great billows surge forth..."

The vast ocean has no time of interruption. The ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* abides eternally; moved by the winds of objective spheres (*viṣaya*), the various waves of consciousness surge forth and arise in succession.
Thus, one should know that the seven consciousnesses are all formed through the transformation of the *ālaya*.

As for the statement that "they are all able to manifest their own respective objects," it means that each of the seven consciousnesses possesses both the aspect of the perceiver (*darśana-bhāga*) and the aspect of the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*).

[They are] divided, because each arises from its own self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*). As for the statement that "there are no real dharmas whatsoever," this negates the existence of a real self (*ātman*) or dharmas external to consciousness.
How do they transform?

It means that through the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination of self and dharmas, when the various consciousnesses arise, they transform and appear as a semblance of a self.
Regarding the Dharma: because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are shrouded by ignorance, they take this [ālayavijñāna] as a basis and grasp it as a real self and real dharmas.

This is like a person suffering from a severe illness whose mind is clouded and who perceives various colors, people, and objects; or like one in a dream, where due to the power of dreaming, the mind manifests as the appearance of various external objects, and during the dream one grasps them as truly existing external things, only to realize upon waking that they were merely transformations of the dream.

When those of external schools first hear the doctrine of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), they do not yet grasp its essential meaning; therefore, this section provides a detailed explanation of the characteristics of the transformation of consciousness.

It refers to how, since beginningless time, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses of sentient beings have erroneously conceptualized a self and phenomena, giving rise to various forms of discrimination.

Infused into the *ālayavijñāna*, they become seeds. When the *ālayavijñāna* gives rise to the seven consciousnesses, each of these seven consciousnesses possesses both a transforming subject (*pariṇāma*) and a transformed object (*pariṇāmya*).
Those transformed objects appear as real selves and dharmas; the sixth and seventh consciousnesses fail to understand them and grasp these appearances as true.
The reason they do not understand is that they are shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*), just as, for example, a craftsman might fashion a ghost at the gate of a temple.
On another day, as he passed by, because of his delusion and intoxication, he mistakenly took it for a real ghost and was struck with terror, unaware that it was originally his own creation.

In this same way, ordinary people who are ignorant and deluded cling to a real self and dharmas, unaware that these are originally what they themselves have habituated and what their own consciousness has manifested.
As for the mention of "other consciousnesses" not being specified, this refers to the first five and the eighth.

Because this grasping does not exist, those who take this grasping to be a real self and real phenomena—namely, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses—universally conceptualize and grasp it with such firm persistence that it cannot be broken.
Just as one suffering from a dream can give rise to false perceptions, the sense organs, the body, and the environmental world that are perceived are entirely transformations of the mind;
apart from the mind, there are no separate sense organs, body, or environmental world, even though they appear to be external.
The appearance of objective phenomena arises, yet in reality they are not external. However, during a dream one grasps them as real, and only upon waking does one realize they are not;

this serves as a metaphor for how ordinary beings are deluded by *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and grasp it as real, whereas the noble ones comprehend *vijñapti-mātra* and thus eliminate such grasping.
My own body is likewise so: it is a transformation of consciousness alone. Due to delusion, one clings to the existence of a self and various objects;
from this, afflictions arise and karma is created, resulting in an endless cycle of birth and death (as explained at length above).
This combines with the previous analogy regarding the grasping at existence during a dream. Within a dream, one grasps at dream-objects as being truly existent;

therefore, within the dream, one may experience sorrow or joy, suffering or pleasure, and various other distinct phenomena. It is exactly the same for those who are deluded regarding *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only):

they grasp at the existence of various external objects, give rise to afflictions, and create karma. (The note stating "as explained extensively before" refers to what was previously discussed in the sections on humans, devas, and the Hīnayāna.)

Regarding the explanations of the causes and effects of good and evil and so forth, from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, all are transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*). The former school did not understand this and merely asserted that they are substantially existent.

Only upon awakening to and comprehending this principle does one realize that one’s own body is a transformation of consciousness alone, and that consciousness is the fundamental basis of the body (the meaning of their lack of understanding will be refuted below).

This accords with the preceding analogy: upon awakening, one knows that [the object] does not exist. Regarding "that which is transformed by consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra-pariṇāma*): "only" (*mātra*) has the sense of exclusion and inclusion.
It excludes phenomena that are substantially existent outside of consciousness, while it includes the phenomena transformed by consciousness; they are not entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, "only" has the sense of determination, meaning that there is definitely nothing but the transforming consciousness. Furthermore, "only" reveals the sense of preeminence. It is not...
There are no mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth; because consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone is predominant, the "king" is cited to include its "retainers. Thus, it is simply called "consciousness.

Consciousness has the meaning of "discerning" (*vijñapti*); since all eight [consciousnesses] discern their objects, this is as explained at length in that treatise. The single phrase "Consciousness is the root of the body" concludes that [the body] is rooted in the objective realm.

The fourth is the Mahāyāna School that Destroys Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This teaching destroys the attachments to the characteristics of the Dharma of both the preceding Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, while secretly revealing the principle of the true nature of emptiness and quiescence.

These discourses on destroying characteristics are found not only in the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, but pervade all Mahāyāna scriptures. Whereas the first three teachings follow a fixed chronological sequence, this teaching destroys attachments as they arise and has no fixed temporal order.

Therefore, Nāgārjuna established two types of *prajñā*: the common and the uncommon. The common is heard, believed, and understood by those of the two vehicles alike, as it destroys their attachment to the Dharma of the two vehicles. The uncommon is understood only by Bodhisattvas, as it secretly reveals the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

The two masters of India, Śīlabhadra and Jñānaprabha, each established a system of the three-period teachings (*tri-kāla-dharma*). Regarding this teaching of emptiness, one [master] claimed it preceded the Vijñaptimātra-Dharmalakṣaṇa teachings, while the other claimed it followed them. For my current purpose, I adopt the latter view.
This pair [of statements] simultaneously refutes the attachments to the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

However, while the subsequent text contains only passages refuting the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) of the Mahāyāna, there are none concerning the Hīnayāna; for once the Mahāyāna has been refuted, how could the Hīnayāna still persist?

If one were to speak of them separately, it would not differ from what preceded; therefore, they are not stated again. Regarding the phrase "refuting attachment," this refers to the Buddha’s provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*).

Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one analyzes the various phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) in order to reveal that they exist only as designations dependent upon conditions.

This is done gradually to lead sentient beings to understand that all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, are fundamentally empty, thereby awakening them to the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Because sentient beings do not comprehend this and instead cling to these phenomena as being fixed and real, the Buddha taught the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to dismantle their attachment to those phenomena as having intrinsic nature.

The attachment to marks is termed the "Teaching that Destroys Marks. This merely eliminates the illness, rather than eliminating the medicine. Regarding the terms "esoteric" (*mi*) and "exoteric" (*xian*), these are used to distinguish it from explicit exposition;
hence, they are called "esoteric-exoteric. The principle of the true nature’s emptiness and quiescence is precisely what is elucidated within the "Teaching that Reveals Nature.
This is the "true emptiness" of wondrous existence, not a mere emptiness. These are the two schools’ interpretations of the meaning of emptiness.

One must examine and know [this] with precision (the commentary clarifies its superiority by distinguishing it according to teaching and according to time). Generally, it is often said: "The *Āgamas* teach the four kinds of existence (*catvāra upādānaskandhāḥ*), while the *Prajñāpāramitā* teaches the eight kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭau śūnyatāḥ*).

However, here we do not point exclusively to the *Prajñāpāramitā* as representing the "destruction of marks" (*lakṣaṇa-bhaṅga*); other sūtras also contain this. For example, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty and quiescent; there is no grasping and no seeing. This emptiness of nature is itself the Buddha; it cannot be conceived or measured. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* states:

"All phenomena, from their very origin, are eternally characterized by quiescence and extinction. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Milk has no nature of curd; stone has no nature of gold. The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like space. It is like the emptiness of the city of Kapilavastu, the emptiness of the Great Nirvāṇa," and so forth. There are also categories such as the "Chapter on Emptiness" in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Nevertheless, all...

In the sūtras, there are passages that refute [the existence of] mental afflictions (*kleśa*); these all belong to the refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This is because this school’s system of classifying the teachings (*śāsana-vibhāga*) does not conform to a fixed chronological order. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the night of attaining the Way until his parinirvāṇa, he constantly preached Prajñā; therefore, it is said that there is no fixed time.

Thus, we know that those who designate the teaching of emptiness as the second period do so from the perspective of one particular class [of practitioners], and it is not an exhaustive account of the truth. Nāgārjuna establishes two kinds of Prajñā: the common [Prajñā] for the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and the uncommon [Prajñā] for Bodhisattvas.

However, there are two types of Śrāvakas: first, the "foolish-dharma" Śrāvakas, who never believe in the Mahāyāna; and second, the "broad-wisdom" Śrāvakas, who partially realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). The *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "Those who wish to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle should study the Prajñāpāramitā."

Regarding the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other sutras, Master Sengzhao stated: "The three vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) to attain the Way. Thus, when a Bodhisattva hears of emptiness, they immediately know it to be the emptiness that is identical with existence; it is merely a negation that implies affirmation. Therefore, they do not cling to the view of emptiness.

This differs from the two vehicles, who, upon hearing of emptiness, become weary of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and fail to generate joy in adorning the Buddha-fields or benefiting others, desiring only to proceed toward quiescent extinction. As for Śīlabhadra and Jñānaprabha, there were differences in their establishment of the teachings according to time. Specifically, at Nālandā Monastery in India, there were two great virtuous masters (*bhadanta*) living simultaneously: one named Śīlabhadra and the other named Jñānaprabha.

Śīlabhadra, relying on sutras such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, established the doctrine of the Three Periods of Teaching (*tri-kāla-dharma*), taking the Dharma-character Mahāyāna (*lakṣaṇa-mahāyāna*) as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). He held that the Buddha’s first period of teaching consisted of the *Āgamas*.

First, there were the teachings on the manifest (vijñapti). In the second period, he taught the Prajñāpāramitā and other sūtras concerning emptiness. In the third period, he taught the Saṃdhinirmocana and other sūtras that clarify the principle of Vijñaptimātra—the teaching of the Middle Way which is neither empty nor existent. Jñānaprabha relied upon such sūtras as the *Suvikrāntavikrāmī* and others.

The *Miaozhi* (Wondrous Wisdom) is the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, or alternatively, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā*. Treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* also establish a three-period classification of the teachings, regarding the signless Mahāyāna as the true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). They state that at the first period, the Buddha taught existence;

at the second period, he taught the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), which is neither empty nor existent, because the faculties [of sentient beings] were still inferior and unable to fully enter the equality of true emptiness. Therefore, only in the third period did he speak from the ultimate perspective, teaching the doctrine of the equality and single flavor of true emptiness—that dependent origination is itself emptiness.

Thus it is said, "each establishes [its own system]," and so forth. Regarding the statement that it is "prior to Consciousness-Only," this is the view of Śīlabhadra; the view that it is "subsequent" is the view of Jñānaprabha. Here, we follow Jñānaprabha’s position, as it intends to refute characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to reveal the nature (*dharmatā*).
Desiring to refute this, one first interrogates them, saying: "If the objects that are transformed are illusory, how could the consciousness that transforms them be real?
This is precisely the refutation of the Dharma-character (Faxiang) teaching. Previously, one gradually refuted the Small Vehicle's attachment to the real existence of dependent origination;

Now, since the attachment to [the notion that things] truly exist has already been dispelled, upon what could a mere conventional designation (prajñapti) possibly be established? Therefore, it is refuted.
First, he summarizes the intent of that school’s position, saying: "Although the objects perceived in a dream do not truly exist, the dreaming consciousness that perceives them does."

Thus, it is not that [the mind] is non-existent; therefore, it possesses the power to transform objects. Now, let us interrogate this by employing the principle of the *Nirākāravāda* (Aspectless School) that both mind and object are empty.
The intent is as follows: the two dharmas of mind and object are established in mutual dependence. Since the object does not exist, how could the mind alone remain?
If one were to say that one exists and the other does not, [the following refutes this by means of that very analogy]: then the dream-mental-conception and the object seen therein should be distinct.

Since he previously cited the analogy of a dream to establish the thesis that objects are empty while consciousness exists, he claimed that dream-objects are non-existent while dream-mental-conceptions exist.
Now, we challenge him using that very analogy, saying: if it is as you have established, then...
The mind and its objects become distinct because one exists while the other does not.
If they are distinct, then the dream is not the object, and the object is not the dream. When one awakens and the dream ceases, the object ought to remain.
He said: "Even if the mind and its object were different, what fault would there be? Therefore, he further challenged him:
"If they were different, then the mind and the object would be mutually contradictory. Why? Because that which is the subject of dreaming is not the same as that which is dreamed of.

Since the dream and the object are neither of them the other, then even upon waking from the dream, the object should still be present—just as when Zhuang Zhou dreamed he was a butterfly; if the butterfly were not part of the dream," [it would have to exist independently].
The dreamer is also not the butterfly. When Zhuang Zhou awakens from his sleep, the butterfly must still be there, because Zhou and the butterfly are two distinct entities.
This can be understood through the Dharma: this is the reversal of that state where the object is empty and the mind exists, resulting instead in the mind being empty while the object exists.
Furthermore, if an object were not a dream, it would have to be a real object;
just as the butterfly dreamed of by Zhuang Zhou—if it were not a dream—it would have to be a real butterfly. If it were a real butterfly, [it would follow that it could not be a dream].

This would result in the objects of cognition being existent, which contradicts the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). A question is asked: "How does this differ from the previous objection? The answer is:

If a dream were not a thing, by what would it have its characteristics?
Just as a dream is not a butterfly, there should be a characteristic of dreaming that exists separately outside of the butterfly. If such a separate characteristic exists, what is its nature?
Thus, his argument is exhausted.
Therefore, we know that during a dream, one conceives of dreams and dream-objects as if there were a distinction between the seer and the seen;

The *Yuánjué chāo* states: "That which is called a dream is simply the originally existing conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*) of a person while awake, which, due to its state of obscurity and contraction, suddenly and falsely manifests the perception of a 'seer' as well as the appearances of the dreamed body and the objects perceived therein;
it is these appearances that are termed a 'dream. Upon this single, false dream," it continues.
There is a distinction between the internal mind and external objects. The internal mind refers to inverted perception;

external objects refer to the body seen in a dream, as well as the ground traversed therein, and so forth. To speak according to ultimate principle, there are no objects apart from the mind, and no mind apart from objects.
Since the objects perceived are, in their entirety, fundamentally empty, how could the perceiving thought-mind alone be existent? Therefore it is said:
"Both are equally false and illusory; neither has any real existence. Furthermore, the objects seen in a dream appear clearly as if they exist, yet do they truly exist?
If one were to say that although the grasping thought ceases upon waking, it does not preclude its existence during the time before one has woken.
Regarding that which "exists": although the objects perceived do not exist once one has awakened, it does not follow that they did not exist while one was unawakened.
If this were so, then object and mind would both exist; why, then, speak of "consciousness-only"? Thus we know that sentient beings possess a fundamentally existing, intrinsically pure true mind;
because they fail to realize it, the three subtle and six coarse [transformations] appear. These are what are referred to as such.
This refers to what is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). Upon this deluded consciousness, there appears a distinction between an internal mind and external objects;

yet in reality, the object is the object of consciousness, and consciousness is the consciousness of the object. When the Buddha taught the principle of consciousness-only in the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), it was because he had not yet revealed the intrinsically pure true mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-tathatā-citta*);
rather, he subsumed it within the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to accommodate those of inferior capacity. [He did so] awaiting...

Only when the roots are matured do the emptiness of both mind and objects become manifest; it is only upon reaching the definitive meaning of the Final Teaching that the original enlightenment of the true mind is revealed.
This is because all things depend upon various conditions and thus lack intrinsic nature.

To speak of them specifically, the sleeping consciousness arises from nine conditions, and so forth. Since they depend upon these various conditions, they lack any real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Therefore, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says: "There has never been a single phenomenon that does not arise from causes and conditions;
therefore, there is no phenomenon that is not empty. It further says: "Phenomena produced by causes and conditions—I declare them to be emptiness.

Regarding the characteristics of all objective realms, a sutra states: "Whatever has characteristics is entirely false and illusory.

the first point asserts that if phenomena were substantially existent, they would not depend on causes and conditions. Since they do depend on causes and conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is the established conclusion.
Next, it means that since phenomena arise through causes and conditions, they are themselves empty; this is not like the "analytical emptiness of phenomena" (prajñapti-śūnyatā) of the Two Vehicles.

From the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), things exist. However, if one approaches it from the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), even the mind that undergoes transformation cannot be apprehended, let alone the objects transformed by it.

To speak directly:

"When those with a perfect capacity receive the teaching, there is no teaching that is not perfect; when those with a partial capacity receive the teaching, even the perfect becomes partial. This is the case if one merely reveals their attachments.

The nature [of beings] does not harmonize with the preceding teachings; thus, they cannot avoid being partial as well. This is truly because there are differences between gradual and sudden faculties, and consequently, differences between deep and shallow teachings.

If one accepts only one [teaching] and rejects the others, how could one possibly fathom the perfect and subtle?
Third, directly revealing the true source (for those who study the Buddha’s definitive and real teachings).
"True source" refers to the awakened nature elucidated by this teaching; it is called "true" because it is not false, and "source" because it is the fundamental basis.

In contrast to the preceding four teachings, it is termed "directly revealing. This means that while the true nature also exists within the previous four teachings, it merely accommodates the capacities of sentient beings through provisional means.

The teaching is not yet directly and clearly revealed. This scripture is spoken by the Buddha according to his own ultimate intent; it is not called "directly revealed" merely because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
Regarding the teaching of the One Vehicle that reveals the nature: it states that all sentient beings possess the true mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) takes the meaning of awakening and realization; that is to say, the single dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) is luminous, clear, and mirror-like in its reflection, its nature having existed from time immemorial.

Therefore, it is called "original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*); this is a name given in contrast to "initial enlightenment" (*ādi-bodhi*). Because it differs from the preceding deluded consciousness, it is called the "true mind.
The statement that "all sentient beings possess it" serves to distinguish [it] from insentient things such as wood and stone.
From time immemorial, it has been eternally abiding and pure; it is luminously manifest and never obscured, clearly and perpetually aware.
This beginningless and eternal abiding is called the "Fundamental" (ben); this luminous manifestation and clear awareness is called "Awakening" (jue).
It is also called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) and also called the Tathāgatagarbha.
"Nature" (*dhātu*) refers to the present cause, while "Buddha" refers to the future fruit. This true mind is the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood;
therefore, it is called Buddha-nature. While "nature" is spoken of generally as encompassing both the sentient and the insentient, here, by speaking of "Buddha-nature," the insentient is excluded.

In essence, "awakening" (bodhi) takes illumination and discernment as its meaning; it is so designated because it pertains specifically to sentient beings. As for the *tathāgatagarbha*: that which is free from inversion is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*);
that which has emerged from the entanglements is called "Come" (*āgata*). "Womb" (*garbha*) is a name signifying concealment and inclusion;

it refers to the cause of sentient beings while still within the entanglements, which contains and encompasses the fruit once they have emerged from them. Although obscured by afflictions, its nature is eternally unchanging.

From beginningless time, it has been obscured by delusive conceptualization; failing to realize this oneself and merely identifying with the ordinary physical substance, one becomes attached to karmic fetters and undergoes the suffering of birth and death.
Sentient beings, due to their delusion regarding the fundamentally enlightened true mind, naturally grasp at the illusory body and mind as "self.
Because they grasp at a self, they give rise to afflictions and create karma, thereby undergoing the suffering of birth and death. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:

"All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions, like a person who has lost their way and mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely identifying the four [directions]."

The "Great" refers to the characteristic of one's own body; the shadows of the six sense-objects as conditions refer to the characteristic of one's own mind. Because of these delusions, one falsely undergoes the cycle of birth and death; therefore, this is called ignorance.

The Greatly Awakened One took pity on them and taught that all things are empty. Furthermore, he revealed and showed that the true, numinous, awakened mind is pure and entirely identical [to the ultimate reality].
When the Buddhas speak of the emptiness of all things, they are shattering deluded attachments. When they reveal spiritual awakening, they are manifesting the true nature.
To be entirely identical with the Buddhas means that the holy and the ordinary are equal, for there is neither increase nor decrease. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "All sentient beings..."
Sentient beings equally possess Buddha-nature; they all share the same vehicle, the same liberation, the same cause and the same fruit, and the same nectar.

All shall attain the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of the cool and refreshing state. The *Qingliang* commentary states: "It is not only that their causes are the same, but their fruits are likewise the same."
Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not fully possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
it is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it."
First, the general purport of the treatise: this constitutes its ultimate thesis. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* cited here refers specifically to the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata.

The Wisdom of the Fruit. The three insights (vidyā) reveal the mutual penetration of self and others. First: there is not a single sentient being who does not possess [Buddha-nature];

thus we know that those without nature do not belong to the category of sentient beings. This refers to things such as grasses and trees, which have already transcended the view of the five natures (i.e., the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

This is the essence [of the teaching]. Therefore, it is said that one has already transcended the views of the five natures. Once [this is] realized (there is no longer the two obstructions of afflictions and the known).

It universally benefits all sentient beings; the Buddha-wisdom is likewise. Regarding "a single mote of dust as a metaphor for sentient beings," there are briefly three meanings: first, because delusion obscures the true; second, because the small contains the great;

Deluded for a long time, they have not seen it; therefore, I must teach them to abandon false conceptualization so that they may personally perceive their own wisdom, just as one might find a great scripture within a shattered atom.

This is the wisdom [of the Buddha]. Generally speaking, the Buddha-dharma relies upon causes and conditions; since both causes and conditions are absent, by what means could awakening be attained?
Yet, they merely cling to illusory appearances and contentedly identify themselves as ordinary beings, whether as animals or humans.
Having already lost track of true nature, one consequently clings to delusion. Because of this clinging to delusion, one remains forever in the lower stream.
Thus, Prime Minister Pei’s *Text on Arousing the Bodhicitta* states: "I possess a true body, which is perfect emptiness and stillness;
I possess a true mind, which is vast, numinous, and cognizant. Yet, I abandon and fail to recognize these, instead recognizing this deluded body."
Reflect: following death, you will follow rebirth; you will suffer shoulder to shoulder with birds, beasts, and various other species.
For one who aspires to be a great man (mahāpuruṣa), is this not shameful? The above has distinguished former delusion.
Now, by tracing this back to the ultimate teaching, one realizes that one is originally a Buddha.

This reveals that the present awakening occurs because encountering the ultimate teaching serves as the superior condition (*pratyaya*), while the arising of the liberating mind within constitutes the cause (*hetu*).

Thus, delusion is understood to be none other than reality; one turns back from confusion to achieve awakening. It is like a wealthy elder, complete with all marks of excellence, who suddenly falls into a deep sleep.
In a dream, one assumes the body of a poor, lowly, and ugly person, begging for alms and undergoing suffering, reaching every extreme. Suddenly, someone calls out and awakens one;
only then does one realize that this was originally a body of merit and virtue, and that the preceding dream-scape was entirely false and illusory.
Thus, Bing Shan said: "The 'Discourse on the Original Person' is precisely the single call of the Awakened One."

Therefore, one must practice in accordance with the Buddha’s conduct and align the mind with the Buddha’s mind. Returning to the root and restoring the source, one cuts off and eliminates ordinary habits.

This speaks of practicing based on awakening and attaining realization. "Practicing in accordance with the Buddha’s conduct" means entering through awakening that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*).

What was previously called "awakening" refers to intellectual understanding (*pariyatti*); what is here called "awakening" encompasses both realization and understanding. Regarding "returning to the root and restoring the source," it is [to be] with...

This refers to the correspondence of essence. Regarding "eliminating the habitual tendencies of ordinary beings": one realizes that delusion is fundamentally empty; thus, there is elimination without anything to eliminate.

What are called "habitual tendencies of ordinary beings" are precisely the two attachments and the two obstacles. Furthermore, these categories of obstacles are threefold: namely, the seeds, the manifest, and the habitual.
Among these three, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are the most subtle. By citing the subtle, the coarse is implied; thus, for the time being, only "habitual tendencies" are mentioned.

However, regarding the explanation of severance and realization according to this school, the *Great Commentary* states: "To illuminate that afflictions have no root is itself the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*). To illuminate that the essence has no self-nature is itself the realization of Suchness (*tathatā*.
This means that when one is deluded, it is called "affliction," and when one is awakened, it is called "wisdom. There is no difference between the essence of affliction and the essence of wisdom.)

Because they are of two aspects, one knows that the nature of delusive afflictions is empty; it is entirely the essence of wisdom. This very essence of wisdom lacks intrinsic nature due to its dependence on conditions.

This nature of lacking intrinsic nature is entirely True Suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, the illumination within stillness is called wisdom, and the stillness within illumination is called Suchness.

When stillness and illumination are fused as a pair, Suchness and wisdom are of one essence. The general meaning of the realization and verification according to the *Shijiao* (Real Teaching) is as follows.
It is so. Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "Neither beginning, nor middle, nor end; it is beyond the reach of words.

Vasubandhu’s commentary on the preceding phrase explains: "This is the characteristic of severing the fetters. This wisdom that exhausts the outflows—is it severed by initial wisdom, by intermediate wisdom, or by final wisdom?
He answers: "It is not severed by initial wisdom, nor by intermediate or final wisdom. As the verse says: "Neither beginning, nor middle, nor end."

Therefore, if that is so, how is it severed? The treatise says: It is like a lamp flame; it is not severed by the beginning, middle, or end alone, because it is apprehended through the prior, middle, and posterior.
That is to say, if one were to apprehend only a single moment, it could not be severed. Only when all three moments are apprehended together can it be said to be severed.
Since severance occurs through these three moments, there is no fixed nature of severance. For if the first moment alone could sever it, the middle and subsequent moments would not be required.

If it were possible to sever [the continuum] later, it would not require the beginning or the middle; since it does require these three times, we know that there is no intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Applying this same critical analysis to each one, none of the three can be severed. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end," because there is no severance throughout these three times.

Only then can one sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Therefore, the *Lun* (Treatise) says: "Because they are grasped in the prior, middle, and posterior [stages]. The Master of the Treatise takes all three times collectively to reveal that there is no severance throughout the three times.

While the Sūtra and the Treatise appear to speak in opposition, their intent actually complements one another. The Sūtra relies on the nature (*svabhāva*), while the Treatise specifically relies on the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Only when nature and characteristics are without obstruction can one sever the fetters. This applies to the Real Teaching (*samyak-śāsana*). If one proceeds directly from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), [the meaning is as follows].

The teaching states: "One obstacle is all obstacles; one abandonment is the abandonment of all. This is because when a single thought becomes deluded, the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) becomes deluded;
yet, when one delusion is severed in accordance with the nature of reality, all are severed. This is due to the identity of the one and the all.

Because they arise in mutual dependence, a single dharma accords with its nature and pervades all things; because its characteristics are indestructible, it does not obstruct the separate severance [of afflictions].
By subsuming the particular within the universal, all of this constitutes the severance and realization of the Huayan Perfect Teaching.
"Diminish it again and again, until one reaches non-action (*wuwei*).

This arises from severing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) to give rise to realization. 'Diminishing' refers to the capacity to sever; 'diminishing it again' refers to dispelling the mind that seeks to sever.

This is because one thoroughly understands that delusion is fundamentally empty, and thus conventionally designates it as 'severing. How could one who clings to the notion of a real, substantial severing [attain this]?"

He has realized the profound mystery; therefore, he simultaneously severs the mind and dispels [all phenomena]. Thus, when both subject and object are equally extinguished, one then accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This "unconditioned" refers precisely to the nature of *tathatā* (suchness). (However, these two lines of text borrow from the Daoist scriptures.

There it says: "In learning, there is daily increase; in the Way, there is daily decrease. Decrease it again and again until one reaches the unconditioned. The meaning there is that those who study worldly affairs strive for much learning and thus have daily increase, whereas practitioners of the Way abandon study and discard knowledge to return to their original simplicity; hence it is called "unconditioned.")
[This is] for the following reason: while the phrasing here is the same, the meanings differ.
The spontaneous application [of wisdom] as vast as the sands of the Ganges is called "Buddha.

When the preceding mind accords with the Buddha-mind, it is identical to the Buddha-body (*dharmakāya*). Now, this reveals the function that is identical to that body, manifesting in every single atom (*rajas*).
Since every thought-moment is perfectly realized, its application is as vast as the sands of the Ganges. For when one is deluded, it becomes the dust-labor of the sands of the Ganges;
yet after awakening, it becomes the wondrous function of the sands of the Ganges. Thus, the *Qingliang Xinyao* says: "Every mind acts as a Buddha;
there is not a single mind that is not the Buddha-mind. Everywhere one realizes the Truth; there is not a single speck of dust that is not the Buddha-land. This is truly because one knows all...
The Dharma is the very nature of the mind; therefore, one attains the accomplishment of the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*) without depending on awakening through another.
One should know that delusion and awakening are of one and the same true mind.

The preceding text extensively explained the characteristics of delusion and awakening, all of which were discussed in relation to persons—that is, when deluded, one is called a sentient being; when awakened...
At that time, it is called "Buddha. That which was deluded is identical to that which was awakened; the single essence of true mind is fundamentally without difference.
